## IN THIS VOLUME
# ON ALCHEMY
### are contained the following:

->By Geber the Arab <note>original: "Gebri Arabis"; Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in early chemistry</note>, a most industrious Philosopher, and most expert in natural things, especially metals:<-
->On the Investigation of the Perfection of Metals. Book I.<-
->Of the Sum of Perfection of Metals, or of the Perfect Mastery <term>Magistery: the successful completion of an alchemical process, or the "Great Work"</term>. Books II.<-
->By the same author: On the Discovery of Truth or the Perfection of Metals. Book I.<-
->On the Construction of Furnaces. Book I.<-

->By Roger Bacon <note>original: "Rogerij Bachonis"</note> the Englishman: a small book on Alchemy.<-
->By John Richard the Englishman: The Correction of Alchemy.<-
->The Lesser Rosary <note>original: "Rosarius minor"</note> on Alchemy, by an unknown author.<-
->The Book of Secrets by John Khalid <note>original: "Ioannis Calid"</note>, son of Jazichus the Jew.<-
->The Emerald Tablet <note>original: "Tabula Smaragdina"</note> on Alchemy by Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure said to have founded the hermetic arts</note> the philosopher, with the commentary of a certain unknown author.<-

->The Mirror of Alchemy <note>original: "Speculum Alchemiae"</note>, by the most learned man Roger Bacon.<-

---

->All these works have been edited from the oldest manuscripts, with the addition of corrections by certain authors, as accurately and correctly as possible.<-

->At Nuremberg, at the house of Johannes Petreius,<-
->IN THE YEAR 1541.<-

# ON ALCHEMY

->the following are contained.<-

By **GEBER** the Arab, a most ingenious Philosopher, and most expert in natural matters, especially those pertaining to metals: On the investigation into the perfection of metals. **Book I.**
On the Sum of the perfection of metals, or of the perfect <term>Mastery</term> <note>The "Magistery" (magisterij) refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process to create the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. **Books II.**

->*All that follows is now printed for the first time.*<-

By the same author: On the discovery of truth, or the perfection of metals. **Book I.**
On the construction of Furnaces. **Book I.**

->ALSO.<-

The Mirror of Alchemy, by the most learned man **Roger Bacon.**
The Correction of Alchemy, by the most learned man **Richard the Englishman.** <note>original: "Richardi Anglici"</note>
The Lesser Rosary, on Alchemy, by an unknown author.
The Book of Secrets of Alchemy, by **Khalid son of Yazid the Jew.** <note>original: "Calidis filij Iazichi Iudæi"; Khalid ibn Yazid was an Umayyad prince traditionally associated with early alchemy.</note>
The Emerald Tablet on Alchemy, by **Hermes Trismegistus.** <note>A foundational hermetic text providing the philosophical basis for alchemy.</note>
The Commentary of Hortulanus the philosopher, upon the Emerald Tablet of Hermes.

*All items have been compared with manuscripts, most carefully corrected, and arranged in a new way according to the intent of the authors, illustrated with necessary arguments and pictures, so that they may deservedly seem to be born anew.*

->**At Nuremberg, by Johannes Petreius,**<-
->**In the Year 1541.**<-

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page is the preface to the 1541 collection "De Alchemia." The author, "Chrysogonus Polydorus," is a pseudonym for Andreas Osiander, a prominent Lutheran theologian who also famously wrote the unsigned preface to Copernicus’s "On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres." He is here defending the study of alchemy as a legitimate branch of natural philosophy.</meta>

# CHRYSOGONUS
## POLYDORUS ON SEVERAL
## SMALL BOOKS ON ALCHEMY <note>original: "ΠΕΡΙ ΧΗΜΕΙΑΣ" (Peri Chemeias)</note>
### Preface to the Reader.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' depicting a pastoral or biblical landscape scene with trees and a figure resting on the ground.</image-desc>When I desired to release several selected small books of the ancients concerning alchemy <note>original: "περι χημείας"</note> from our library to the printers to be published, so that a greater benefit might flow from them to students of Philosophy, I judged that I ought to say something by way of preface. For I do not doubt that many, though indeed good men, yet unskilled in the nature of things, may think that this entire branch of art should be utterly despised and covered in silence; either because they believe it to be completely false, or more difficult than can be investigated with such great labor and uncertain outcome. 

But as for me, although I was once of that same opinion, being drawn by the desire for learning, I have diligently examined this class of authors as the opportunity arose. I gained so much knowledge of things from them that I not only congratulate myself significantly, but also do not hesitate to recommend that others come to know them as well. For since all Philosophy either directs speech <note>Referring to Logic and Rhetoric.</note>, forms morals <note>Referring to Ethics.</note>, or inquires into the secrets of nature—and since the care of speech exists for the sake of something else, and the rule of morals is now sought from elsewhere than Philosophy <note>Likely referring to Theology or Scripture as the source of morality in the Reformation era.</note>—who does not see that that part of Philosophy which explains the natures and causes of things is the most excellent? 

Moreover, metals are no small portion of the nature of things, which no part of human life can do without without loss, since they are the tools of all craftsmen, the price <term>precia</term> <note>Meaning currency or the basis of value.</note> of all things, and the ornaments of all dignities. I say nothing of the fact that they also provide medicine abundantly and supply various colors for painting; otherwise, they would be subjects of great wonder even by the mere contemplation of them. Therefore, whether the knowledge of their nature is more useful or more pleasant, decide <note>The word "constitue" is split across the page break.</note> with me...

<meta>catchword: stitue= (completing the word "constitue," meaning 'decide' or 'determine')</meta>

<summary>In this preface, Andreas Osiander (writing as Polydorus) defends the study of alchemy and metallurgy as the most excellent branch of philosophy because it reveals the hidden causes of the natural world.</summary>
<keywords>Andreas Osiander, alchemy, natural philosophy, metallurgy, medicine, pigments, value of metals</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the preface by Chrysogonus Polydorus (Andreas Osiander). Having established that alchemy is a branch of natural philosophy, he now addresses the poor literary style of medieval alchemical texts and warns against the many "scoundrels" (con-artists) who exploit the art’s reputation to defraud the public.</meta>

-># PREFACE TO THE READER.<-

<sig>aa 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: ne</meta>

I cannot yet determine. Aristotle and both <note>Likely referring to Aristotle and his successor Theophrastus, who are mentioned later in the paragraph.</note> (for it is fair to believe so) wrote about these things; if their works survived, perhaps there would be no need for those dedicated to the study of Philosophy to lower themselves to this class of authors. But since those ancient works are now lost, nothing else remains from which we may draw a certain and exact knowledge of these matters. 

If anyone is offended by the impurity of language or the unrefined "barbarism" <note>Humanist scholars of the 16th century often looked down on the "Barbarous" Latin used by medieval scientists, which they found clunky compared to classical Roman style.</note> in this genre of writing, they should consider that throughout the ages, very few have existed who combined significant knowledge of things with eloquence. Nor should such a precious treasure be neglected, or even cast aside, because of the inconveniences of the language. For it is worth the effort to hear these most ingenious men—relying partly on the principles of Philosophy, partly on the evidence of experience, and indeed often on both—discussing this art, and the entire nature of metals. 

Specifically, they discuss what the primary and immediate matter of metals is, what their efficient cause is, and how they differ among themselves—whether by some substantial form <note>The essential nature that makes a thing what it is.</note> or only by accidents <note>Non-essential qualities like color or hardness.</note>. They also investigate which metals have affinities for one another, whether one can be transformed into another, and how they ought to be brought to the highest perfection. 

In inquiring into all these things and many others of this kind, or in asserting with great constancy and authority that they have already discovered them, these authors bring so much light and knowledge that I would not unwillingly doubt whether even Aristotle or Theophrastus could have provided as much. Therefore, this so remarkable addition to Philosophy should not be neglected or despised by students, even if it must be begged for here and there from a "barbarous" class of writers, and collected like gold from dung <note>original: "aurum è stercoribus." A classical metaphor (attributed to Virgil) for finding wisdom in unpolished sources.</note>. 

There is also another significant reason why you might wish to know these authors. For since the fame of this art has already filled the world, many scoundrels <note>original: "nebulones"</note> wander about everywhere professing it. Though they know nothing of the art, they rob simple people—who are greedy for both profit and this admirable art—by leading them on with empty hope and using either theft or fraud. No one will detect their wickedness, fraud, and trickery more quickly, nor convict them more effectively, than one who has penetrated into the inner shrines <note>original: "adyta," referring to the most sacred, private part of a temple.</note> of this art. For this art, without a knowledge of Philosophy—

<summary>Osiander defends the "barbarous" Latin of medieval alchemists, arguing their scientific insights on the nature and transformation of metals are as valuable as those of Aristotle. He also suggests that studying genuine alchemy is the best way to detect the many fraudsters (nebulones) preying on the public.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle, Theophrastus, nature of metals, transformation, substantial form, accidental form, fraud, alchemical style, gold from dung</keywords>

-># PREFACE<-

<meta>catchword: ænigma-</meta>

...not <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "which those [scoundrels] cannot feign."</note> (which those men cannot feign) happens to no one else, and it provides such certain and effective tests for true gold and silver that no fraud, however clever or hidden, can be applied to them that this art does not detect and utterly destroy. This is also of great interest to the State <note>Latin: *Reipublicæ*. Referring to the public good or the Commonwealth.</note>. Since authors of this kind enrich Philosophy and expose counterfeiters—who are harmful to the State—they would be worthy of recognition even if the art itself were worth nothing.

And yet, I see no reason why we should not believe the art to be true. For it is reasonably asserted by men most practiced in Philosophy; and certain craftsmen, without any obvious reason for deception, have confirmed that they discovered it, swearing by all things sacred, even in published books. Testimony is also given by the emotions of the mind: the joy and gladness of a spirit exulting at the discovery of the art, bursting forth so vehemently that it is not believable that such a performance could be feigned by any mere acting. 

It also has the testimony of history. For Suidas <note>Referring to the *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the Mediterranean world, formerly attributed to an author named "Suidas."</note>, an author by no means to be despised, writes that the Egyptians, relying on wealth gained from this art, sought to stir up revolution <note>Latin: *res novae*, literally "new things," a common idiom for political rebellion or upheaval.</note> and were restrained by Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor (r. 284–305 AD).</note>. I will recount his words: 

Chemistry (he says) is the manufacture of gold and silver. Diocletian searched for and burned the books of this art because of the uprisings the Egyptians had stirred up against him. He treated them harshly and murderously. It was then that he searched for and burned the books written by the ancients concerning the chemistry of gold and silver, so that wealth should no longer come to the Egyptians from such an art, and so that they, emboldened by an abundance of money, should not rebel against the Romans in the future. <note>Original Greek: "Χημεία (inquit) ἡ τοῦ χρυσοῦ καὶ ἀργύρου κατασκευή, ἧς τὰ βιβλία διερευνισάμενος ὁ Διοκλητιανὸς ἔκαυσε... [etc.]"</note>

That is what he says. Nor do these accounts differ from other historians describing Diocletian. Moreover, the ancient Poets have shown not only that this art existed, but even how it is to be practiced, [revealing it] most perfectly through very charming fables, but...

<summary>Osiander defends the legitimacy of alchemy, citing its ability to detect counterfeit metals and a historical account from the Suda regarding Emperor Diocletian burning Egyptian alchemical books to suppress a rebellion.</summary>
<keywords>alchemy, gold and silver, counterfeiting, Diocletian, Suidas, Suda, Egypt, history of chemistry, statecraft</keywords>

-># TO THE READER<-

<sig>aa 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: arma=</meta>

...they nonetheless suggested [this art] **enigmatically** <note>original Greek: αἰνιγματικῶς (ainigmatikōs). Meaning through riddles or allegories.</note>. For what else is the **Golden Fleece**, sought by the Argonauts from Colchis, than the investigation and sketching out of this art? About this, Suidas <note>Referring to the *Suda*, a 10th-century encyclopedia.</note> says elsewhere: *“This is reported not as a poetic fable, but it was a book written on skins, containing how gold ought to be made through chemistry. Therefore, the people of that time rightly called it the 'Golden Fleece' because of the power derived from it.”* That is to say, this is not spoken of as a fiction, but there was a book, written on parchment, containing the method by which gold must be made through Chemistry. Deservedly, therefore, the men of that age called it the Golden Fleece, on account of the efficacy which was drawn from it.

The Golden Fleece is not given to Jason unless he first undergoes certain and dangerous labors; that is, unless he first learns the **practice** <note>original Greek: πράξιν (praxin). Referring to hands-on laboratory work rather than just theory.</note> by exercising his own hands. For he who is ignorant of the practice possesses a book written about this art in vain. Furthermore, the dangerous voyage indicates the difficulty of investigating the "matter" of the **philosophers' stone** (as they call it). Because this matter takes the place of earth and is metallic, it is called the **Field of Mars** <note>The *Ager Martius*; Mars was the planetary and mythological equivalent of Iron/Hard metals.</note>, after Mars the god of metals. And because it must be purged, prepared, and perfected in fire so that it is fit to receive the "seed," it is depicted as being plowed and cultivated by **fire-breathing bulls**.

These **Bulls** are the **furnaces**, which, unless they are correctly built and provide a continuous fire of the proper amount, either the matter is ruined, or the vessels are destroyed, and the craftsman is struck by a noxious smell, or even perishes in a fire. Next, the **ever-watchful Dragon** is **quicksilver** <note>Latin: *argentum vivum*; Mercury.</note>. The **Dragon's teeth** are **sublimated mercury** <note>Mercury that has been heated into a vapor and cooled into a solid, purified form.</note>, because it possesses the whiteness of ivory, the hardness of bone, and an incredible "biting" quality <note>Latin: *mordacitatem*. Likely referring to its corrosive or reactive properties.</note>, not without poison. While it is being sublimated, it is caught in a glass vessel very similar to a helmet (which the Arabs call an **alembic** <note>A chemical still used for distillation.</note>); thus the Dragon's teeth are brought to Jason in a helmet, so that he may scatter them in the place of seed into the Field of Mars. For Mercury must be sublimated from that earth repeatedly until it is "fixed" within it. While this happens, it rises from the earth in the manner of little spears, some of which are upright, some leaning, some completely horizontal, and as if aimed at the throats of enemies; they continually grow in length so that they seem to move, and they display the appearance of a very dense army just now most fiercely clashing. Therefore the [armed] men...

<summary>This page presents an alchemical interpretation of the myth of Jason and the Golden Fleece, arguing that the story is an allegory for the chemical process of creating gold. It identifies specific mythological elements, such as the fire-breathing bulls and dragon's teeth, as symbols for furnaces and sublimated mercury.</summary>

-># PREFACE<-

<meta>catchword: periti (those skilled)</meta>

...they are imagined to be born armed, only to fall by mutual wounds—that is, to finally be fixed and buried in that earth. And unless the vessel were made of glass or flint, without any pores, the craftsman would be in peril from being breathed upon by the odor. For this reason, Jason is imagined in Ovid’s account to have turned the danger away from himself and onto his enemies by means of the flint. Thus far, the **philosophers' stone** is perfected; what remains is to lull the ever-watchful dragon to sleep. That is, to convert **quicksilver** <note>original: "Argentum uiuum." Mercury, the "living silver."</note> by the stone's efficacy into gold or silver. When this succeeds, the victorious Jason carries off the **Golden Fleece**—which is to say, the Craftsman has attained this most precious art.

But before this is done, they sacrifice to Hecate in the manner described by Orpheus. In this sacrifice, a great mystery lies hidden. Furthermore, because the same philosophers' stone is also said to heal human bodies, and to keep them healthy and unharmed until the very end of life, Medea is therefore imagined to restore Jason’s father to youth. This art is also suggested by the Gardens of the Hesperides and the story of Cadmus; and Cadmus, having sought immense wealth from it, founded Egyptian Thebes. Let no one wonder, then, that this art flourished most especially in Egypt. 

These are great testimonies of this art, but far greater are those which the Jews bring from the Sacred Scriptures, according to the unique properties of the Hebrew language. For they say that this art is also a part of their **Cabala** <note>Kabbalah: Jewish mystical and esoteric tradition, which the author here links to secret chemical knowledge.</note>. They claim that the Prince of Tyre, mentioned in Ezekiel, practiced it; and therefore the prophet reproaches him because, through his confidence in that art, he seemed to himself to be a God. For the prophet (as they say) relates that the gold and silver he held in his treasures had not been dug from the earth, nor demanded from his subjects, nor snatched from enemies, but that he had made it for himself, relying on this very art. It is for this reason that he is said there to be wiser than Daniel, and to have surveyed all the secrets of nature. 

Likewise, they assert concerning their ancestors that the prophet Hosea reproached them for the abuse of this art when, speaking in the person of God, he said to them: *“I multiplied silver for them, and they made gold for their idol.”* And so that you might believe this more firmly, they say that David, in the twelfth Psalm (according to their numbering), provides a certain taste of this art's evidence when he says: *“The words of the Lord are pure words, silver burned in an <term>aludele</term> in the earth, or dust, refined seven times.”* <note>Psalm 12:6. Standard Bibles usually translate this as "silver tried in a furnace of earth," but the author uses a technical alchemical term.</note> For this is how they interpret it word for word—whether rightly or otherwise, [those skilled] in that language...

<summary>The author continues interpreting Greek myths (Jason, Medea, Cadmus) as alchemical allegories before moving to biblical proofs. He claims that the "Prince of Tyre" and the ancient Israelites used alchemy to create gold, citing specific Hebrew interpretations of Ezekiel, Hosea, and the Psalms.</summary>
<keywords>Jason and the Argonauts, Medea, Cadmus, Kabbalah, Prince of Tyre, Ezekiel, Hosea, Psalm 12, aludel, transmutation, longevity</keywords>

->TO THE READER.<-

(let the experts judge.) And they add: No one is so foolish that they would wish to treat silver in such a way—since it is a task of the greatest labor and highest industry—unless, having been so treated, it became more precious. Nor would the prophet compare the word of God to such silver, but rather to pure gold, unless such silver were equal in power to gold. <note>The author refers to Psalm 12:6, "The words of the Lord are pure words: as silver tried in a furnace of earth, purified seven times."</note> And this certainly agrees closely with the words of **Geber**, who says of silver: "He who knows how to further refine it, and after refinement to thicken and fix it, shall join it with gold," etc. <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in medieval alchemy.</note> We have said these things in such a way that we do not greatly desire to persuade. For if there is any solid truth here, philosophical minds will recognize and grasp it no less sluggishly than a healthy eye perceives light, or a magnet attracts iron.

There are roughly four kinds of writers in this art. Some follow a Method, without figures and riddles, in the philosophical manner; but they cover the material of the <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note> in such a way that no one, except by the gift of God, may understand what they intend. In this category, **GEBER** holds the first rank, whom certain more recent authors follow at a long distance, such as **Roger Bacon** (whom our own **Pico della Mirandola** also mentions) and many others. 

Some involve the entire art, though shaped methodically, in riddles, as the poets do in the fables of Cadmus, the Hesperides, and the Argonauts, and as a certain more recent author does in the dialogue concerning the "Golden Book." 

Others, omitting the method, overshadow only the principal points with figures and riddles in such a way that they wish to be understood only by those who have made such progress in Philosophy that they might almost divine this art by themselves. Of this kind are **Hermes**, **Maria the Prophetess**, **Morienus**, and the ***Assembly of the Philosophers***. <note>original: "Turba philosophorum," one of the oldest Latin alchemical texts, portraying a debate between Greek philosophers.</note>

The fourth kind writes only of the <term>practice</term> <note>original: "πρᾶξιν" (praxin), meaning the hands-on laboratory work.</note> but so simply and rustically that nothing hidden appears to be within. But in that category, there is absolutely "nothing sound" (as the proverb says), <note>original: "οὐδὲν ὑγιές" (ouden hygies), a Greek idiom for something being unreliable or corrupt.</note> but all things are found to be erroneous, false, and full of lies. 

Students should begin primarily with **GEBER**. He wrote four small works that bear witness to one another: namely, *Of Investigation*, *Of Invention*, *Of Furnaces*, and the *Sum of the Perfect Mastery*. Certain people have corrupted this last work in various ways, dividing it into three, five, or seven books, when there are only two. Having compared the copies, we have provided a version as corrected as possible, and most diligently distinguished—

<summary>This preface categorizes alchemical authors into four styles of writing and identifies Geber as the primary authority for students. It emphasizes that true alchemical knowledge requires divine favor or deep philosophical insight to pierce through intentional riddles.</summary>
<keywords>Alchemy, Geber, Roger Bacon, Pico della Mirandola, Hermes Trismegistus, Maria Prophetissa, Morienus, Turba Philosophorum, Philosopher's Stone, Alchemical Practice</keywords>

# PREFACE TO THE READER.

...having completed this, we shared it with friends. We would have also added the *Book of Roots* <note>original: "Librum radicum"</note> attributed to him by many, but we have most clearly discovered it to be the work of another. It remains for us to advise the reader regarding the name of this art, which I am surprised Erasmus calls by the barbaric and monstrous name "Alcumistic." It is, however, called by its true name by the Greeks: *Chemeia* <note>original: "XHMEIA"</note>, that is, the "Art of Casting" <note>original: "Fusoria"</note>, because metals and things related to them—namely salts, alums, and vitriols—flow in the fire and are chiefly treated in this art. They are called *chymata* <note>original: "χύματα"</note>, that is, "fusible things," from the word *cheo* <note>original: "χέω"</note>, to pour or melt (just as from *cheo, cho, chymata* are derived). The Arabs, however, borrowing this name from the Greeks, prefixed an article according to their custom and called it "Alchemy." In the same way, they called Ptolemy’s composition *Megiste* <note>original: "Μεγίστην", meaning "The Greatest"</note> by the name *Almegist* or *Almagest*.

This art, like all others, has certain peculiar words and terms not well known to the common people. This is partly because they are barbaric and exotic, such as *Aludel* <note>a pear-shaped condensing vessel</note>, *Alembic* <note>a distilling apparatus</note>, *Bearded Botus* <note>original: "Botus barbatus", likely a specific type of crucible or digestion vessel</note>, *Alkali salt*, *Elixir*, and the like. Partly it is because they are used catachrestically <note>original: "καταχρηστικὰ", meaning used figuratively or improperly</note> or abusively; for example, "to imbibe" <note>original: "Imbibere"</note> instead of to moisten; "to fix" and "fixation" <note>original: "Figere & Fixare"</note> instead of making a substance so that it is not destroyed or evaporated in the fire; "to descend" <note>original: "Descendere"</note> instead of to melt down and clarify; and many others of this kind, which will become known only through a diligent reading of the authors. Having said these things in the preface, I will no longer delay the well-disposed and studious reader, who (unless I am mistaken) has long been panting with an eager mind for the inner shrines of this admirable art.

->The end of the preface.<-

# PREFACE TO THE READER.

...having completed this, we shared it with friends. We would have also added the *Book of Roots* <note>original: "Librum radicū"; likely referring to a foundational chemical or linguistic text</note> attributed to him by many, but we have most clearly discovered it to be the work of another. It remains for us to advise the reader concerning the name of this art, which I am surprised Erasmus calls by the barbaric and monstrous name "Alcumistic." Its true name among the Greeks is *Chemeia* <note>original: "ΧΗΜΕΊΑ"</note>, that is, the "Art of Casting" <note>original: "Fuforia"</note>, because it deals with metals and things related to them—namely salts, alums, and vitriols—which flow in the fire and are chiefly handled in this art. These are called *chymata* <note>original: "χύματα"</note>, meaning "castings," from the word *cheo* <note>original: "χέω"</note>, to pour (just as from *cheo* comes *cho* and *chemata*). The Arabs, however, borrowing this name from the Greeks, prefixed an article according to their custom and called it *Alchemy*. In the same way, they called Ptolemy’s "Greatest Composition" <note>original: "Μεγίστην"</note> the *Almagest*. 

This art, like all others, has certain peculiar words and terms not well known to the common people. This is partly because they are foreign and exotic, such as **Aludel** <note>a pear-shaped condensing vessel</note>, **Alembics** <note>the cap of a still used for distillation</note>, **Bearded Botus** <note>original: "Botus barbatus"; likely a specific type of crucible or digestion vessel</note>, **Alkali salt**, **Elixir**, and the like. Partly it is because they are used figuratively <note>original: "καταχρηστικά"; catachrestic or misused terms</note>, such as **To Imbibe** for "to moisten"; **To Fix** or **To Fasten** for "to bring it about that the matter is not destroyed or evaporated in the fire"; **To Descend** for "to melt and liquefy"; and many others of this kind, which will become known only through a diligent reading of the authors. 

Having said these things in the preface, I will no longer delay the well-disposed and studious reader, who (unless I am mistaken) has long been panting with an eager spirit for the inner shrines of this admirable art.

->End of the preface.<-

The investigation of this most noble science—born from continuous and frequent diligence in labor, and from an excessive zeal equal to it, as well as from our deepest thoughts and various connected ideas—I shall hand over to you. This is so that the subsequent volumes may be better and more clearly understood by you, and so that, once understood, and through ingenuity and scrutiny applied to them, they may be more easily and promptly brought to fulfillment. And because it is one thing to investigate the theory <term>rationem: the underlying logic or theoretical framework of the art</term> of the art, and another to attempt and test the subtleties and ingenious devices of these things until, by working, scrutinizing, and experimenting, the complete goal is reached. # ON INVESTIGATION

We have previously written before our book, which is entitled *The Height of Perfection in the Mastery* <note>original: "Summa perfectionis magisterij"; a foundational medieval alchemical text attributed to Geber</note>: in which we have completely determined, according to the order of science, whatever we have seen and touched. This was done according to experience and certain knowledge, which we noted through our own scrutiny regarding the effects of natural and mineral things, and the various transforming properties appearing in the work. We have endeavored to reveal our science, previously composed, along with this commentary on investigation, which we have composed to explain that very science. Therefore, by right, this book precedes the other, since through this book I seek to investigate the knowledge of the thing that brings about perfection.

# THE PERFECTION OF GEBER
<note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of early chemistry.</note>

...long and tempered decoction <note>A process of heating or "cooking" a substance in a liquid</note>, thickened and fixed in the bowels of the clean earth, produced with the preservation of its radical moisture—which is not corrupting, but leads to a solid substance that is fusible with the proper application of fire and extendable under the hammer. By defining this perfecting nature, we can more easily arrive at a knowledge of the corrupting thing. And that is to be understood in the opposite sense: namely, an impure substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"; mercury</note> and sulfur, mixed without due proportion, or insufficiently decocted in the bowels of an unclean earth, neither rightly thickened nor fixed, possessing a combustible and corrupting moisture, and of a thin and porous substance; or having fusion without the proper application of fire, or none at all, and not sufficiently enduring the hammer.

I have found the first definition embedded in these two bodies, namely in the Sun <note>original: "Sole"; the alchemical term for Gold</note> and the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical term for Silver</note>, according to the perfection of each. But the second definition is found in these four, namely in tin, lead, copper, and iron, according to the imperfection of each. And because these imperfect bodies cannot be reduced to health and perfection unless the opposite is worked within them—that is, that the manifest be hidden and the hidden be made manifest—which operation or reversal is done through preparation, therefore preparation must be applied to them. To prepare, then, is to take away the superfluous, to supply what is absent, and thus to bestow upon them the mark of perfection. However, the perfect bodies do not lack this preparation. They do, however, require such preparation that their...

Preparation, therefore, consists of removing the superfluous and supplying what is lacking in imperfect bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" usually refers to the seven metals: gold, silver, mercury, copper, iron, tin, and lead.</note>, which cannot be done without the assistance of manual labor and purifying agents. ### On the things that assist preparation, and their cleansing, Chapter 4.

The things that assist in preparations are these: namely, all kinds of salts, alums, vitriols <note>original: "atramentorum," referring here to sulfate minerals used in making inks and acids</note>, also glass, borax, and those things which are of this nature, as well as very sharp vinegar and fire. With these, we propose to prepare the imperfect bodies; however, it is fitting to first cleanse them if any impurity exists within them, according to our experience, in which we have been made certain through the aforementioned things.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for purifying chemical substances, following the general introduction to "Investigation" or laboratory research. The focus here is on the purification of various salts and alums.</meta>

<header>ON INVESTIGATION</header>

### The Purification of Common Salt.

Common salt <note>Sodium chloride</note> is purified in this manner:
First, let it be burned <note>calcined or heated to high temperatures to remove organic impurities</note>; once burned, let it be dissolved in warm common water; once dissolved, let it be filtered through a cloth; once filtered, let it be congealed <note>evaporated until crystals form</note> over a slow fire in a glazed dish; once congealed, let it be calcined for a day and a night in a moderate fire, and keep it thus sufficiently purified.

### The Purification of Alkali Salt.

Alkali salt <note>Potassium carbonate or soda ash</note> is purified just like common salt, and it is the "fat of glass" <note>original: "sagimen uitri," a term for the scum or dross produced during glassmaking, rich in alkaline salts</note>. First, let it be ground, and the whole dissolved in warm common water; afterwards, let it be filtered, congealed, and calcined with a slow fire.

### The Purification of Salt Gem.

First, let it be ground; then, let it be treated in the same way as common salt. <note>Salt gem refers to rock salt or halite, often found in transparent, jewel-like crystals.</note>

### The Purification of Sal Ammoniac.

First, let it be ground with a preparation of purified common salt. Afterwards, let it be sublimated <note>heated until it turns to vapor and reforms as a solid</note> in a tall aludel <note>term: aludel; a pear-shaped subliming pot used in alchemy</note>, until the pure substance has been totally extracted. Afterwards, let it be dissolved upon a porphyry stone <note>a hard igneous rock used for grinding and chemical reactions</note> in the open air, if you wish to make a "water" <note>liquid solution</note> from it, or keep it as a sublimated and sufficiently pure solid.

### The Purification of Other Salts.

Various other kinds of salts are still to be found, which are prepared and purified by the method already described.

### The Purification of Alums.

First, concerning glacial alum <note>likely potassium alum, which has a glassy or "icy" appearance</note>. Many things can be [accomplished] through it...

# THE PERFECTION OF GEBER <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most influential figure in early Islamic alchemy; this text represents the "Summa Perfectionis," a foundation of medieval chemistry.</note>

cannot be prepared without some cleansing of the substance itself. However, it is cleansed in this manner: Let it be placed in an alembic <note>A vessel consisting of two parts used for distillation: a boiling flask and a cooling cap.</note>, and let all the moisture be extracted from it, which is of great value in this art. The dregs remaining in the bottom of the vessel should either be dissolved upon a stone in some damp place, or in the water extracted from it, or they should be set aside.

->The Cleansing of Jamen Alum.<-

Jamen alum <note>original: "alumen Iameni"; likely referring to alum sourced from Yemen, prized for its purity in dyeing and alchemy.</note> is prepared in the same way as ice-like <term>glaciale</term> <note>A transparent, crystalline form of alum.</note> alum, except that in this art it possesses greater power.

->The Cleansing of Other Alums.<-

Many other alums are still to be found, all of which are prepared and cleansed as previously described.

->The Cleansing of Inks.<-

First, concerning black ink <note>original: "atramento"; in this context, it refers to vitriol or metallic sulfates used to make pigments and acids, rather than writing ink.</note>. Black ink is cleansed thus: First, let it be dissolved in clean vinegar, afterwards let it be distilled and coagulated. Or, let it first be placed in an alembic and the total moisture be extracted. The dregs calcined <note>Reduced to powder through heat.</note> in this distillation should be dissolved upon a porphyry stone or in their own water, and then coagulated. Or, the water itself may be reserved according to the will of the craftsman.

->The Cleansing of Copperas.<-

Copperas <note>original: "cuperosa"; ferrous sulfate, often called green vitriol.</note>, or vitriol, is cleansed just like black ink. However, black ink has a greater earthiness than green ink.

->The Cleansing of Other Inks.<-

There are various inks, and they are found in different colors; these are cleansed as described above.

# ON INVESTIGATION

## Concerning glass and boraxes.

Glass <note>original: "vitrum"</note> and boraxes, if they have been made in the proper manner, do not require any further preparation.

## The purification of very sharp vinegar.

Furthermore, vinegar <note>original: "acetum"</note> of any kind, whether sharp or sour, is refined and purified, and its strength or effectiveness is improved through distillation <term>distillation: the process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then cooling the vapor to create a purified liquid</term>. We have treated their cleaning and purification sufficiently [elsewhere]; with these substances, the imperfect bodies <note>The "imperfect bodies" usually refer to base metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron, which alchemists sought to "perfect" into gold or silver</note> can be prepared, purified, improved, and refined, always by means of the appropriate fire.

# On the preparation and improvement of bodies in general. Chapter V.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap letter 'P' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or alchemist, within a landscape containing a tree and foliage.</image-desc>
These bodies are prepared and purified by these means toward the intention of the fire, in this manner. They also possess an unclean, drossy, and combustible earthiness that is too coarse, which hinders their penetration and fusion. These and such things are the superfluities in these aforementioned bodies, which have been discovered in them through our experience and certain, ingenious investigation. # THE PERFECTION OF GEBER
<note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most celebrated alchemist of the Islamic Golden Age, whose works formed the foundation of European chemistry.</note>

Since the removal of accidental qualities is possible, we must use an artificial fire <note>likely a controlled furnace or "Athanor"</note> upon these aforementioned cleansed materials to take away all superfluous accidents, so that only the substance of the quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"</note> and the radical sulfur remains. And this is the complete preparation of the imperfect things, and their perfect purification. The improvement, purification, and refinement of these substances—of the pure substance remaining—is done in many ways, according to what the elixir requires.

The method of preparation and purification in general is this: First, all the superfluous and corrupt humidity in their essence must be raised up <note>evaporated or sublimated</note> with a proportional fire, as well as the subtle and burning superfluity; and this is done by calcining <note>term: calcination; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve oxidation or dehydration</note>. Then, the total remaining corrupt substance in their lime <note>original: "calce"; the powdery residue left after heating</note>—consisting of burning humidity and blackness—must be corroded away with those aforementioned cleansed corrosive, sharp, or bitter things, until the lime is white or red, or colored according to the nature and property of the body, and clean, and pure from all the aforementioned superfluity or corruption. And these are cleansed with those corrosives by grinding, soaking, and washing.

Afterward, however, the total unclean earthiness and the combustible and coarse dregs must be deleted or cast down. This is done with the aforementioned things, either cleansed or pure, which do not have a metallic fusion <note>melting point</note>, mixed and well-ground with the aforementioned lime prepared in the manner described. In the fusion, or the reduction of the lime, these will retain with themselves the coarse and unclean earthiness mentioned before, while the body remains pure, cleansed from every corrupting superfluity.

# ON INVESTIGATION

From this entire descent, the method for the Improvement <note>original: "Melioratio"</note> and refinement <note>original: "subtiliatio"</note> of these pure substances in general is as follows. First, this body, having been purged and reduced, must be calcined <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to drive off volatile impurities.</note> again with fire and the aforementioned cleansing aids; then, it must be dissolved with those substances that are solvent. For this water is our stone, and "living silver" <note>mercury</note> from living silver, and sulfur from sulfur, abstracted and refined—or thinned—from the spiritual body. This can be improved by strengthening the elemental virtues within it using other preparations of its own kind, and by increasing the color, fixation, weight, purity, fluidity, and all other things that pertain to the perfect elixir. And this is the method, investigated by us alone, for the preparation, purification, refinement, and improvement of mineral bodies in general. Now let us pass to the special or particular preparation of any imperfect body, with all its methods, and also of the perfect mineral body. And first, concerning Jupiter <note>The alchemical name for the metal Tin.</note>.

## On the preparation of Gold. Chapter X.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'P' featuring intertwined leafy vines and floral motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
Truly, perfect bodies do not require preparation as far as their perfection is concerned, since they are already perfect; however, so that they may be further refined and thinned, such a preparation must be applied to them: Take Gold <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical name for Gold, literally "the Sun"</note> beaten into thin plates, and place it layer by layer with well-prepared common salt in a calcination vessel. Place it in the furnace, calcining <note>term: calcination; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical state, often to a powder</note> it well for three days, or until the whole has been finely calcined. Then let it be taken out, ground very well, washed with vinegar, and dried in the sun. Afterward, let it be ground well with half its weight of cleansed salt ammoniac <note>term: sal ammoniacus; ammonium chloride, used as a flux and to help dissolve metals</note>, and set to dissolve until the whole, by the benefit of the common salt and the salt ammoniac, has been dissolved into a most clear water. This is the ferment for the red elixir, a precious thing, and a true body made spiritual.

### On the properties of the Great Elixir.
### Chapter XII.

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial letter 'I' featuring two figures, likely scholars or alchemists, seated within a decorative frame of foliage and scrolls.</image-desc>

Now we have sufficiently determined the preparation of the imperfect bodies and the refinement of the perfect ones, so that any discerning person may fulfill their intention regarding them. Let one therefore attend to the properties and the modes of action in the composition of the Great Elixir <term>Elixir maioris: the "Greater Work" or Universal Medicine capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</term>. For we seek to make one single substance, yet one gathered from many things, united and fixed, which, when placed upon the fire, the fire does not drive out. It must be mixed with melted metals and liquefy with them, by means of that which is in it of an entering substance <note>the ability to penetrate the metal</note>, and be mixed by that which is in it of a mixable substance, and be consolidated by that which is in it of a consolidating substance, and be fixed by that which is in it of a fixing substance. It must not be burned by those things which do not burn gold and silver, and it should bring about consolidation and weight with the proper and perfect application of fire. However, do not understand "a short time" to mean that it can be completed on the first attempt in a few days or hours. Rather, it is because, in comparison to other modern physicians <note>likely referring to other alchemists or "doctors" of the art</note> and even in respect to the operation of nature, the truth is reached more quickly in this way. Whence the philosopher <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus or Aristotle, frequently cited as "The Philosopher" in alchemical texts</note> said: Medicine is of its own time.

However, those things which we have extracted with our own fingers through our experience, and have seen with our eyes, and touched with our hands, we have written in the *Summary of our Perfect Mastery* <note>original: "Summa nostri perfecti magisterii"; a foundational medieval alchemical text attributed to Geber</note>. Therefore, let the wise craftsman study our volumes, gathering together our scattered intentions which we have set forth in various places—lest it be made public to the wicked or the ignorant—and let him test what is collected, until through study and experimenting with the ingenuity of labor, he arrives at total knowledge through persistence. Therefore, let the craftsman exercise himself, and he shall find the method of this investigation (his innermost heart being moved by love) through our consideration, which also gives full knowledge of the truth regarding the matter and form of that which perfects and that which corrupts.

For in our investigation, we have considered the matter of perfect things <note>referring to "perfect" metals like gold and silver</note> along with their form, from the root of their mixing unto their completion, to be pure, without any intervening corruption. We have also considered, from the opposite perspective, that the substance of imperfect things and perfect things is everywhere one and the same: namely, quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; mercury</note> and sulfur; which, before their mixing, are pure and clean. And through this consideration and our own practice, we have found that the corruption of imperfect things has arrived accidentally, giving a new and corrupted form to the matter. For when we saw the imperfect bodies prepared through our experience and our ingenuity, and cleansed of all superfluous corruption and fleeting impurity, or freed from the earthy, we found them to be of greater clarity.

<summary>The author explains that the "perfect" and "imperfect" metals share the same fundamental substances—mercury and sulfur—and that the flaws in base metals are merely accidental impurities that can be removed through diligent labor.</summary>

### The division of this first book into four parts. Chapter II.

<note>The ornamental letter P marks the beginning of the formal outline of the treatise.</note>
First, therefore, we shall briefly set forth for you all the impediments by which a craftsman is hindered in his work from reaching the true goal; we shall also speak of the necessary conditions for a practitioner of this art <note>The "art" referred to here is alchemy, often called the "Great Art" or "Magistery" in medieval texts</note>. Second, indeed, we shall dispute against the ignorant and the sophists <note>original: "sophistas" - here meaning those who use clever but false arguments to deceive</note> who, on account of their own ignorance and lack of skill in seeking the mastery and profit of this art, destroy the art in the meantime and contend that it is nothing. We shall, however, set forth all of their arguments, and afterwards we shall most evidently destroy them, so that it may be opened clearly enough to prudent men that none of their sophistries contain the truth. Third, we shall dispute over the natural principles which concern the intention of nature; and likewise over the manner of their generation and their mixing with one another by the work of nature, and over their effect, according to the opinion of the ancient philosophers. Fourth, we shall truly show the principles which are toward the intention of our own work, in which we are able to imitate nature, and the manner of mixing and altering—namely, that which is agreeable to nature—along with its causes, to be brought back to the intent of our work.

### The Division of Obstacles. Chapter III.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'S' depicting a scholar seated in a chair, facing left.</image-desc>
There are, therefore, two general types of obstacles attending this work: namely, natural inability, and the lack of necessary funds, or occupations and labors. However, we say that natural inability is manifold. Specifically, it arises from the part of the craftsman's physical organs <note>original: "organi artificis"; referring to the physical body and senses as tools of the soul</note>, and from the part of the soul. From the part of the craftsman's organs, it is also manifold: either because the organ is weak, or entirely corrupted. Finally, from the inabilities of the soul, it is manifold: either because the soul is perverse within the organs, possessing no rectitude or reason within itself on account of those organs—such as the soul of a madman or a fool—or because it is prone to fantasies, improperly receptive to contrary forms, shifting suddenly from one piece of knowledge to its opposite, and likewise from one desire to its opposite.

## On the external impediments that hinder the work of this art. Chapter VI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'R' featuring floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>

We have reduced to two chapters all the impediments that delay the goal of this art, which arise from the root principles according to the nature of the practitioner of this most precious business. It is necessary, therefore, that we finally recount the impediments arriving from the outside, arising from the contingencies of fortune and chance, by which this most glorious work is hindered. We see, therefore, certain astute and ingenious men, by no means ignorant of the works of nature, who follow her principles and works wherever possible; men whose investigation is not based on fantasy in all things regulated by the motions and actions of nature beneath the lunar circle <note>The "sublunary sphere" refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, where things are subject to change and decay, unlike the eternal heavens</note>. These men, however, are oppressed by extreme poverty; due to a lack of resources, they are forced to set aside this most excellent Mastery <note>original: "Magisterium"; the completion of the alchemical process</note>. There are also many others besides those just mentioned who are curious but held back by various cares and anxieties of this kind, occupying themselves entirely with worldly business, from which our precious knowledge flees utterly. Now, therefore, it is sufficiently clear to you from the preceding chapters what the distracting impediments are that lead away from this art.

### Epilogue of this first part, regarding what kind of 
### practitioner is required. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'C' depicting a figure (likely a scholar or alchemist) seated in a natural landscape with trees and a building in the background, enclosed in a square frame with floral motifs.</image-desc>We conclude, therefore, from what has already been said, that it is necessary for the practitioner of this work to be learned and perfected in the sciences of natural philosophy. For no matter how much money or naturally profound talent he possesses, or how great his desire for this craft, he will nonetheless not reach its end unless he has acquired natural philosophy through formal teaching. This is because whatever is not attained through natural talent is remedied by the deficiency being supplied through instruction. It is necessary, therefore, for the practitioner to be aided by the deepest scrutiny and natural industriousness. For despite how much knowledge he might acquire through teaching, unless he is also aided by natural industriousness, he will not be invited to the feast of so precious a thing <note>The "feast" is a metaphor for the successful completion of the Great Work or the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Indeed, through his own industriousness, he might correct his error in an instant—an error for which he would not know how to apply a remedy if he were grounded in teaching alone. Similarly, he might quickly remedy an error through the knowledge acquired by natural teaching, which he could not avoid through industriousness alone; for art is aided by talent, and talent is likewise aided by art. It is also necessary for him to be of a constant will in the work, so that he does not presume to try now this way, now that; for our art does not consist in, nor is it perfected by, a multitude of things. For there is but <term>one stone</term> <note>lapis unus: the singular substance from which the Elixir is derived</note> and <term>one medicine</term> <note>medicina una: the final transformative agent</note> in which the mastery consists, to which we add no foreign thing.

# THE HEIGHT OF PERFECTION BY GEBER

At a great price <note>The "price" here refers to the investment of time and resources</note> (if you are not ignorant of the principles of the art, and have correctly understood those things which we have handed down to you), you shall arrive at the completion of the mastery. For most miserable and unhappy is he to whom God, after the end of his work and labor, always denies the sight of the truth; because he always concludes and terminates the span of his life in error. Such a man, established in labor and obsessed by every perpetual misfortune and unhappiness, loses all the consolation, joy, and delight of this world, and consumes his life in sorrow without profit.

Similarly, when he is engaged in the work, let him study to fix in his mind all the signs which appear in any decoction <note>term: decoction (the process of heating or boiling a substance in a liquid to extract its essence)</note>, and to inquire into their causes. These, therefore, are the things which are necessary for the craftsman suitable for our art. If, truly, any one of these things which we have narrated should be lacking in him, let him not cling to this art.

# THE SECOND PART OF
## THIS FIRST BOOK, IN WHICH ARE
### recounted the arguments of those who deny this art, 
### and then indeed they are refuted.

### General division of the topics to be discussed. Chapter VIII.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'Q' depicting a scholar or cleric seated at a desk within a decorative architectural frame.</image-desc>Since we have already provided you with a single summary of this little book of ours, including all the obstacles to this work, and have given you sufficient instruction for adhering to this art <note>The "art" referred to here is likely alchemy or a related hermetic science</note>, it is now appropriate, according to the intention of our proposal, to argue against the sophists and the ignorant. First, we shall set forth their own arguments, according to what we promised from the beginning that we would determine. Finally, we shall indeed destroy them all, so that it may be revealed to wise men by clear demonstration that those arguments contain nothing of the truth.

### Various arguments of those who simply deny the art. Chapter IX.

In humans and other living creatures, where the physical composition is delicate, the "perfecting principle" <note>The force that completes or brings a thing to its full state of being.</note> is not merely a matter of proportion, nor the substances being mixed, nor the qualities of those substances, nor the blending that results from their mutual action and passion—which arises from the gathering of those primary qualities. Therefore, although these living things have a delicate mixture, we do not know how to "perfect" them <note>In this context, to create or complete them through alchemy.</note>, because we do not know how to infuse the perfecting principle, which is the soul. From this it is clearly evident that it is not a defect in the mixture itself that prevents us from creating an ox or a goat, but rather a defect in the infusion of the soul. For if we followed the path and course of nature according to our craft, we would know how to create both weak and strong compositions.

In **metals**, however, the perfection is of a lesser degree than in living things; their perfection revolves more around proportion and composition than anything else. Therefore, since their perfection is less than in the other things we have described, we can perfect them more freely, whereas we cannot do so with living beings. Thus, God, the Most High and Glorious, has diversified perfections from one another in many forms. Indeed, some believe this art is found in the <term>spirits</term><note>In alchemy, "spirits" refers to volatile substances that can be vaporized by heat, such as mercury, sulfur, and arsenic.</note>. Others, however, look for it in the <term>bodies</term><note>The "bodies" refer to the solid, non-volatile metals like gold, silver, iron, lead, copper, and tin.</note>. Others still seek it in salts, alums, nitres, and boraxes. Some even affirm that this art and <term>mastery</term><note>original: "magisterium" — the complete process or the "Great Work" of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note> can be found in all vegetable things. Among all these seekers, some have judged and handed down this divine mastery to posterity partly well and partly poorly, while others have done so entirely poorly.

It was only through the gathering of truth from their manifold errors—by means of difficult and laborious caution, long and tedious experience, and the investment of great expense—that we succeeded. Their errors frequently warred against the disposition and reasoning of our own mind, and nearly brought us to despair. May they be cursed forever, for they left behind blasphemies and curses for those who followed; out of their own error, they poured over those studying philosophy not the truth, but rather a diabolical instigation after their deaths.

And I myself should be cursed, unless I correct their errors and deliver the truth in this science, as this true art better requires. For this mastery does not need a speech that is entirely hidden, nor one that is completely manifest. We shall therefore deliver it in such a language that it will not be hidden from the wise; yet to the mediocre, it will be most profound, and for the foolish, it will unreachably shut off both ends of the path within this one and the same tradition of ours.

We respond to them briefly, therefore, and say that they understand little in this matter and have very little wisdom, because they suppose that sulfur alone is our material. Quicksilver and sal ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux</note> have the most; sulfur has less; its companion <note>likely arsenic or a similar mineral</note> has even less; fourthly, marchesite has still less; fifthly, magnesia has less than that; and sixthly and finally, Tutia has the least of all.

Each of these participates in "flight," some more and some less. Because of this volatility, certain experimenters have suffered a violent delusion in their preparations and in their projections as well. Therefore, they argue against the art and dismiss it, just as those who base their arguments on sulfur do. We respond to them in the same way we responded to those who assume the nature of sulfur.

It is not permitted to lie. However, all those previously mentioned, being in error, proposed a single material of their own and assumed no other besides it. All of these have now been refuted. Yet many others, almost infinite in number, who create a composition of all these things—or of certain things under a different proportion—proceed in ignorance and lack of knowledge. Their error extends to infinity, since the diversity of the proportions of mixable things is infinite, and the diversity of the mixable materials is infinite. In both of these infinities, it happens that one errs infinitely, sometimes by excess and sometimes by deficiency, though in these cases correction is possible. But we, sparing ourselves the length and wordiness of long speeches, do not wish to dwell upon infinite matters, because we shall hand down universal knowledge in brief statements, by which they might evidently be able to amend the infinity of their errors and correct them. Now, however, let us first discuss the natural principles according to their causes, as we made you attentive to from the beginning and by the mention of them.

### On Sulfur. Chapter XXVIII.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'D' featuring a seated scholar or alchemist figure within a decorative frame of scrolls and foliage.</image-desc> We say, therefore, that Sulfur is the fatness of the earth, thickened in the mine of the earth by a temperate decoction <note>A slow, steady heating process similar to simmering.</note> until it becomes hardened and dry; and when it has been hardened, it is called Sulfur. Indeed, sulfur has a homogeneous and very strong composition, and is of a uniform substance in its parts, being "homeomerous" <term>homeomera: a philosophical term meaning that every part of a substance is identical in nature to the whole</term> because it is homogeneous. Therefore, its oil is not taken away from it by distillation, as it is from other things that possess oil. Those, therefore, who seek to calcine it <note>To reduce a substance to powder through high heat.</note> without losing anything of its substance worth caring about, labor in vain; for it is not calcined except by great industry and by dissipating much of its substance. For out of a hundred parts, you will scarcely reserve three for yourself sufficiently after calcination. Likewise, it cannot be fixed <note>To "fix" a substance is to make it non-volatile so it no longer evaporates when heated.</note> unless it is first calcined; nevertheless, it can be mixed, and its flight <note>Evaporation or sublimation.</note> can be somewhat retarded, and its burning can be repressed, and it is more easily calcined when mixed. He, therefore, who seeks to draw out the work from it should not draw it out by preparing it by itself, since it is perfected with a mixture, and without that, the mastery is prolonged even unto despair. And with its companion <note>Likely referring to Mercury, the other primary alchemical principle.</note> it becomes a tincture <note>A substance capable of transmuting and coloring metals.</note> and gives the complete weight to every metal.

### On Arsenic. Chapter XXIX.

It remains for us to determine the nature of Arsenic for the present. We say, therefore, that it is of a subtle matter, and similar to sulfur; therefore, it need not be defined differently than sulfur. However, it differs from sulfur in this: that it is a tincture <note>A substance used to change the color or quality of a metal</note> for whiteness easily, but for redness with great difficulty; whereas sulfur is a tincture for redness easily, but for whiteness with great difficulty. Furthermore, there are two kinds of sulfur and Arsenic: namely, the yellow and the red, which are useful to this art, while many other kinds are not. Arsenic is fixed <note>rendered non-volatile or resistant to heat</note> just like sulfur. The sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note> of both is better when done from the calxes of metals <note>original: "metallorum calcibus"; the powdery metallic oxides remaining after heating</note>. However, sulfur and Arsenic are not the perfecting matter of this work. For they are not complete unto perfection, though they provide a helping hand <note>original: "adminiculum"; a support or aid</note> toward perfection in certain cases. The bright, scaly, and easily split variety is chosen.

Gold is a heavy metal, yellow in color, malleable, fusible, and capable of withstanding the tests of the cupel <note>original: "cineritij"; a vessel used in refining gold or silver</note> and the cementation process. From this definition, you may conclude that a substance is not gold unless it possesses all the defining causes and characteristics of gold. However, whatever substance thoroughly colors a metal lemon-yellow, brings it to a state of equilibrium, and cleanses it, creates gold from any kind of metal. Therefore, through the workings of nature, we have determined that copper can be changed into gold by artifice. For we have seen in copper mines where water was flowing out, carrying very thin scales of copper with it. This water, by its long and continuous flow, washed and cleansed them. Then, once the water ceased to flow, we saw these scales—mixed with dry sand—baked for three years in the heat of the sun, among which the truest gold was found. We estimated, therefore, that they had been cleansed by the benefit of the water, and through the heat of the sun in the dryness of the sand, the substance was equally digested <note>a term for slow heating or maturation</note> and reached a state of equilibrium. While we imitate nature as much as we can, and alter substances similarly, we are not able to follow nature perfectly in this regard. Gold is also the most precious of metals and is a tincture of redness, because it colors and transforms every body. It can be calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> and dissolved, though without practical utility <note>likely referring to the loss of its metallic form</note>, and it is a medicine that brings joy and preserves the body in youth. It is broken most easily with Mercury <note>referring to the formation of an amalgam</note> and is worn down by the odor of lead. ### On the Moon, or Silver. Chapter XXXIII.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial S featuring scrolling floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>
Since the chapter on the Sun <note>Gold</note> has been set forth, let us direct our discourse toward the Moon, commonly called silver. We say, therefore, that silver is a metallic body, white with a pure whiteness, clean, hard, resonant, enduring in the cupel <note>original: "cinericio" — a vessel used to refine precious metals by burning off impurities</note>, extendable under the hammer, capable of being heated, and fusible. It is likewise calcined <note>Reduced to powder by heat</note> and dissolved with great labor, but with no utility.

Let us likewise deliver a chapter concerning Lead, and let us say that lead is a metallic body, livid <note>bluish-gray</note>, earthy, heavy, and "mute" <note>referring to its lack of resonance or "ring" when struck</note>. Through this, it is therefore evident that tin is more similar to the perfect metal. Lead is likewise burned and becomes minium <note>red lead or lead tetroxide</note>, and when placed over the vapors of vinegar, it becomes ceruse <note>white lead or lead carbonate</note>. And although it does not closely approach perfection, we nevertheless easily make silver <note>original: "argentum"</note> from it through our artistry; it does not retain its own weight in the transformation, but is changed into a new weight. All of this is acquired through the mastery of the art. Lead is also the test of silver in the cupel <note>original: "cineritio"; a vessel used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals</note>, the reasons for which we shall explain.

### On Jupiter, or Tin. Chapter XXXV.

Not omitting the tradition of Jupiter <note>The planet Jupiter is the alchemical symbol for Tin</note>, we signify to the sons of doctrine that it is a metallic body, white, not pure, livid, and sounding little <note>Referring to the "tin cry," the crackling sound made when bending the metal</note>, participating in a small amount of earthiness; possessing a creaking sound, softness of melting without needing to be heated to a glow, and velocity in its root <note>The "root" refers to its fundamental chemical composition</note>; it does not withstand the ash-test <note>cupellation</note> or the cementing-furnace, but is extensible under the hammer.

Jupiter is therefore among those metals diminished from perfection, yet in the root of its nature it is closely related to the more perfect bodies, namely the Sun <note>Gold</note> and the Moon <note>Silver</note>—more so to the Moon, and less so to the Sun. This will be clearly narrated in what follows. Because Jupiter received much whiteness from the root of its generation, it therefore whitens all non-white bodies. However, it has this vice: it makes every body brittle <note>original: "frangit," referring to the tendency of tin to make alloys brittle</note>, except for Saturn <note>Lead</note> and the purest Sun.

And Jupiter adheres strongly to the Sun and the Moon, and therefore is not easily separated from them by examination. It receives the tincture of redness, and shines in it with inestimable brightness, and acquires weight in the mastery of this art. It is hardened and cleansed more easily than Saturn. And whoever knows how to remove its vice of brittleness will suddenly rejoice in the enjoyment of its profit. For it is compatible with the Sun and the Moon, and shall never be separated from them.

### Concerning Mars, or Iron. Chapter XXXVII.

<note>The initial 'M' is decorated with ornate foliage and a stylized human face.</note> The account of Mars <note>The alchemical name for Iron</note> and its whole secret is from the work of nature, because it is a metallic body that is very livid, yet slightly reddish, participating in a non-pure whiteness; it is hard, ignitable, and fusible—though not by a direct fusion—extensible under the hammer, and very resonant. Mars is, however, of hard handling because of the powerlessness of its melting; but if it is melted by a medicine that changes its nature, it is joined to the Sun and the Moon, and is not separated by the trial <note>The assaying process</note> without great industry; but if it is prepared, it is joined, and not separated—

There are two things that must be determined: namely, the principles of this mastery, and the perfection of the same. Perfection, however, consists of the consideration of those things by which it is attained, the consideration of the assisting materials, and the consideration of the thing itself which ultimately completes the work, and by which it is known whether the mastery was present in the perfection or not.

The consideration of those things by which the completion of the work is reached involves the study of the manifest substance, the manifest colors, and the weight in each of the bodies to be transformed. It also includes those bodies which are not to be changed from the root of their nature without that artifice, and likewise the consideration of those in their root with the aid of artifice. Furthermore, one must consider the principles of bodies according to their depth—both hidden and manifest—according to their nature without artifice, and likewise with artifice.

For if the bodies and their principles were not known in the depth of their nature and in their manifest state, both with and without artifice, one would not know what is superfluous in them and what is diminished; for which reason it would be necessary that we never reach the perfection of their transformation.

The consideration of the things assisting perfection is the study of the natures of those things which we see adhering to bodies and causing change without artifice. ### On Sublimation, and why it was invented. Chapter 39.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P with foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>
Proceeding therefore with our purpose, we speak of sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a solid until it becomes a vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify "spirits"</term>. And the cause of its invention was because neither our ancestors, nor we, nor those who will come after us, have found anything that could be united with the [metallic] bodies, except for the spirits alone, or something that contains within itself the nature of both body and spirit.

### What sublimation is, and concerning the three degrees of fire to be observed in it. Chapter 40.

<note>The decorative initial D depicts a classical figure amidst floral scrollwork, marking the start of the chapter.</note>

We say, therefore, that Sublimation is the elevation of a dry thing by fire, with it adhering to its vessel. Sublimation is indeed diversified because of the diversity of the spirits to be sublimated. For some are done with strong ignition, some with a medium fire, and some with a diminished fire. If, therefore, arsenic or sulfur is sublimated, it is necessary that they be sublimated by a diminished fire; since they have very subtle parts joined uniformly to thick parts, their entire substance would otherwise ascend without any purification—indeed, it would be blackened and scorched. Therefore, so that one may separate

# THE SUM OF PERFECTION BY GEBER
<note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, a foundational figure in early chemistry and alchemy.</note>

...unclean earthy substance, it is necessary to devise two types of ingenious methods: namely, the proportioning of the fire, and the purification through mixing with dregs <note>original: "fecum"; refers to the solid residue or waste matter left after distillation or filtration</note>. This is because mixing with the dregs captures the coarse parts and keeps them pressed down at the bottom of the *aludels* <term>aludel: a pear-shaped pot or condenser used in the sublimation process</term>, not permitting them to ascend. Therefore, it is necessary for the craftsman to apply a triple degree of fire to the sublimation.

The first degree is proportioned in such a way that only the altered, cleaner, and more lucid parts ascend through it, until he clearly sees them purified from earthy dross by this means. The second degree is so that whatever remains of their pure essence within the dregs may be sublimated with a greater expression of fire—namely, with the ignition of the *aludel* and the dregs themselves, which he will be able to see with his own eyes.

The third degree, however, is that a very weak fire should be administered without the dregs to that which has already been sublimated and purified, so that hardly anything of it ascends. Whatever does ascend from it is an extremely subtle matter which is of no value in this work, because that is the substance through which burning <term>adustio: a technical term for the scorching or chemical "burning" that ruins a preparation</term> occurs in sulfurs.

Therefore, the entire intention of sublimation is this: that once its earthiness is removed through the proper administration of fire, and once that extremely subtle and smoky part (which brings about burning and corruption) is likewise cast away, there remains for us that part which consists in a state of balance. This part achieves a simple melting over the fire without any burning, and without fleeing from the fire or bursting into flame. That the most subtle part is indeed the cause of burning is proven by the most manifest arguments.

Because fire converts into its own nature each of those things which is most closely related to it, and because from every combustible thing that which is subtle <note>In alchemy, "subtle" refers to matter that is refined, thin, or volatile, as opposed to "gross" or dense matter.</note> is more related to it, and that which is even more subtle is still more related; therefore, that which is the most subtle of all is the most closely related. This is similarly shown by experience, since sulfur or un-sublimated arsenic is ignited most rapidly, though sulfur more easily. However, once it has been sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor and then collecting the cooled solid deposit.</note>, it does not ignite directly, but instead flies away and is thinned out without flaming, though melting occurs first. From these things, therefore, it is clear that our discourse is truthful.

### *On the dregs of metallic bodies, the spirits to be added in sublimation, and their quantity and quality. Chapter 41.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial P featuring vine and floral scrollwork within a square frame.</image-desc>

For that material to which they are more closely united is more powerful in retaining the dregs of the things to be sublimated than one to which they are not. There is, therefore, nothing else that can take their place.
