If the operator has placed the materials, but then fails to increase the heat proportionally, nothing will rise through the process of <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a solid until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again in a purified form</note>. However, how one should determine that heat has already been sufficiently explained to him. Furthermore, if he has used a small quantity of material, or if it was not prepared from a <term>calcined body</term> <note>original: "corporum calce"; metal or mineral reduced to a powder through heating</note>, and he fails to find the correct proportion of heat, the substance will rise in its entirety <insert>without the desired separation</insert>. I have likewise provided a sufficient explanation for discovering this proportion.

Errors can similarly occur regarding the furnace itself; for a large furnace produces a great heat, while a small one produces little, provided that the wood and the openings of its <term>air-holes</term> <note>original: "auricularum"; literally "little ears," referring to the vents or draft holes in the furnace</note> are proportional. Therefore, if one places a large quantity of the substance to be sublimated into a small furnace, it will not be able to provide sufficient heat for the elevation. If, however, one puts a small quantity into a large furnace, the excess of heat will destroy the sublimation.

In the same way, a thick-walled furnace provides a dense and powerful heat, while a thin-walled one provides a thin and weak heat, in both of which errors can occur. Likewise, a furnace with wide air-holes gives a bright and great fire, while one with narrow ones gives a weak fire. Furthermore, if the distance of the vessel—in its fitting to the furnace—is greater from its <term>supports</term> <note>original: "spondilibus"; the ledges or brackets that hold the vessel over the fire</note>, it will produce a great heat; but if the distance is smaller, it will produce less. In all these matters, the greatest errors can occur.

The <term>rectification</term> <note>The correction or proper adjustment of the process</note> of these things is as follows: the furnace should be constructed according to the intensity of the heat required. That is, it should be thick-walled with unobstructed air-holes and a significant distance between the <term>aludel</term> <note>original: "aludelis"; a pear-shaped chemical vessel used to collect the products of sublimation</note> and the supports of the furnace, if a great heat is sought. If a moderate heat is needed, let him find a moderate proportion in all these things; if a weak heat, let him find the same proportion in these...

However, one special practical experience found in the sublimation of bodies is good to consider: namely, that there should not be a large quantity of the body to be sublimated in the bottom of the aludel <note>A pear-shaped chemical vessel used for sublimation.</note>, because a great mass hinders the process. ### Concerning Descension, and the method of purifying
### by means of lozenges. Chapter XLIX.

<note>The title refers to "descension," a process where substances are melted and filtered downward through a vessel, and "pastillos," which are small medicinal or chemical cakes or lozenges.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'N' within a square frame, depicting a seated figure, possibly an alchemist or scholar, working at a desk or with instruments.</image-desc>

Now that the purposes of sublimation have been recounted along with all their causes, it remains for us to demonstrate the method of Descension <note>original: "Descensionis," a process of downward filtration or melting</note>, likewise with its causes and its determined and complete order. The reason for its invention was threefold. One, namely, so that when some matter is enclosed in that vessel which is called the chemical descensory <note>original: "descensorium Chemiæ"</note>, it may descend through its opening after its fusion, and by its descent we may be certain that it has undergone fusion. Another reason is so that weak bodies <note>In alchemy, "weak" or "imperfect" bodies usually refer to metals like lead or tin that melt or oxidize easily</note> may be protected from combustion by this process after their reduction from their calxes <note>original: "calcibus," referring to the powdered oxides produced by heating metals</note>. For when we attempt to reduce weak bodies from their calxes, we cannot reduce every part of them at one time. If, therefore, that part which was first reduced into a body were to wait for the reduction of the whole, the greater quantity of it would vanish through the fire. It was necessary, therefore, to devise a way so that as soon as a part is reduced, it is removed from the fire. This, moreover, is done through the descensory. There is also a third cause for its invention: the purification of bodies from every foreign thing. For the fused body descends clean, and leaves every foreign thing in its cavity. Therefore, since descension was invented for these three necessities, let its method be determined with its instrument previously identified along with its causes. We say, therefore, that its form shall be such that its bottom is sharp—

<note>The text describes a "descensory," a vessel used in alchemy and metallurgy where molten metal or substances are filtered or drained downward through a hole in the bottom to separate them from impurities.</note>

The vessel and its walls should be finished smoothly and without any roughness, tapering down to the sharpness of the base, so that each of the fusible materials can descend freely toward the hole at the bottom without sticking. Its cover (if necessary) should be shaped like a flat dish <note>original: "parapsidis," a shallow bowl or side-dish</note> and should fit it well. These should be made of good, firm earth <note>refractory clay</note> that does not easily crack under the pressure of the fire. Therefore, let the material intended to be melted down be placed into it, supported upon round rods made of earth so that they sit closer to the upper part of the base. Let it be covered and the joint sealed, then placed in a charcoal fire and blown upon with bellows until the entire substance descends into the vessel placed beneath it. However, if the substance is difficult to melt, it can be placed upon a flat or slightly concave plate from which it can easily flow down when the head of the descensory is tilted, once it has fused. For by this means, bodies <note>metals</note> are purified.

But they are purified even better by means of a **pastille** <note>a small cake or pellet of mixed materials</note>, the method of which is the same as the purification by the descensory. For this reason, we are excused from using the former by the latter. Indeed, it holds back the dross of the metals just like the descensory, but better; therefore, we shall describe its method.

*We say, therefore, that we take the body which is intended to be cleansed, and we reduce it into very small grains, or filings, or into a lime <note>original: "calcem," referring to a powder produced by calcination or heating</note> (which is more perfect). We mix with it some other lime which is not intended to be melted, and afterwards we melt it. We find that by repeating this many times, bodies are cleansed—not with that perfect purification which we know to be the ultimate perfection, but with a useful purification, such as medicine—*

### On Distillation and its causes, and on the three types of the same: namely by the alembic, the descensory, and by the filter. Chapter I.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'C' featuring floral scrollwork and foliage.</image-desc>

It is fitting, therefore, that following our proposed plan, we deliver a discourse on distillation along with its causes. Distillation is, therefore, the elevation of aqueous vapors within their own vessel. Distillation is thus diversified. For some is done by fire, while some is truly without fire. That which is done by fire is found to be of two kinds. One is by elevation into an alembic <note>Alembic: a classic distillation apparatus consisting of a boiling pot and a cooling cap with a tube to collect condensed liquid</note>, and the other is by descent <term>Chemistry: here referring specifically to the "descensory" method where liquid is forced downward through heat</term>, by means of which oil is drawn out from vegetables. The reason why distillation was invented, and the general cause for the invention of any distillation, is the purification of a liquid from the dregs of its own turbulence, and its preservation from putrefaction <note>original: "putrefactione"; the process of decay or decomposition</note>. For we see that a thing distilled by any kind of distillation is made purer and is better guarded against rotting.

The specific reason, however, for the invention of that distillation which is done by ascent into an alembic, is the quest for pure water without earthiness. The proof of this is that we see water distilled in this way has no dregs. The reason for the invention of pure water was the "imbibition" <note>Imbibition: the process of a solid substance absorbing a liquid, often used in alchemy to "nourish" a dry material</note> of spirits and cleansed medicines; so that whenever we require an imbibition, we may have pure water which does not leave behind dregs after its own resolution, by which dregs our medicines and cleansed spirits might be infected and corrupted. Truly, the reason for the invention of that distillation which is done by descent, was the extraction of oil pure in its own nature, because by ascent...

### On Calcination, both of bodies and of spirits, with its causes and methods. Chapter 51.

Therefore, after the account of distillation, let us hand down our discourse concerning calcination. Calcination is, then, the reduction of a substance to powder by means of fire, through the removal of the moisture that holds the parts together. The reason for its invention is so that the burning sulfurous quality, which corrupts and defiles, may be destroyed by the fire. It varies, however, according to the diversity of the things to be calcined.

Thus, bodies are calcined, and spirits are calcined, as well as other things foreign to their nature, though with different intentions. Because there are imperfect bodies of two types—namely the Hard, such as <term>Venus</term> <note>original: "Venus"; the alchemical name for Copper</note> and <term>Mars</term> <note>original: "Mars"; the alchemical name for Iron</note>, and the Soft, such as <term>Jupiter</term> <note>original: "Iuppiter"; the alchemical name for Tin</note> and <term>Saturn</term> <note>original: "Saturnus"; the alchemical name for Lead</note>—all of these are calcined. It was necessary for them to be calcined with different intentions, specifically general and special. Yet, in a general sense, they are calcined with one intention: that the corrupting and defiling sulfurous quality may be destroyed by fire. For in this way, every burning sulfurous quality from any substance is burnt away, which cannot be destroyed without calcination. Since the body itself is solid, and because of its solidity and the hiding of the concealed sulfurous quality within the continuity of the substance of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi"; Mercury, considered by alchemists to be the "mother" or base of all metals</note>, it is defended by that solidity from being burnt. Therefore, it was necessary to break its continuity so that the fire, reaching more freely to every tiny part of it, might be able to burn the sulfurous quality out of it, and so that the continuity might not defend it—

<margin>The purity of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"; mercury</note> in it.</margin> Similarly, the common intention in that process is the purification of the earthiness. The reason for the discovery of the calcination of spirits <note>Volatile substances like sulfur, arsenic, or mercury that "flee" the fire.</note> is so that they may be better fixed <note>Rendered non-volatile or stable in heat.</note> and more easily dissolved into water. For every kind of calcined material is more fixed than that which is not calcined, and is of easier solution. Because the parts of the calcined material, having been made more subtle through the fire, are more easily mixed with waters and converted into water. And if you test this, you will find it to be so.

The calcination of other things, however, contributes to the requirements for the preparation of spirits and bodies, which will be determined more extensively by us in the following pages. None of these things, however, belong to the final perfection. Therefore, the method of calcination itself is diverse, owing to the diversity of things to be calcined. For bodies are calcined differently than spirits or other things. And bodies that differ from one another are likewise calcined in different ways. For soft bodies have one general method for the purpose of calcination; namely, that both can be [calcined] by [fire] alone.

The method for these metals, which is perfected by the sharpness of salt, is as follows: a quantity of salt should be thrown over their surface, repeatedly adding more during the melting process. The method for Venus <note>term: Venus; the alchemical name for Copper</note> and Mars <note>term: Mars; the alchemical name for Iron</note> is the same as each other, yet different from the previous metals, and this is due to the difficulty of their melting. Because of the great quantity of earthiness in them, and the great measure of burning and fleeting sulfurousness, they are easily brought into a lime by this method. Through this, therefore, it is left behind, the parts become thinner, and are converted into ash through the discontinuity of that thinness. # THE SUMMA OF PERFECTION BY GEBER

->The nature of salts and similar substances is to be soluble.<-

For in considering all the works of this art, we find that nothing is dissolved except those things. Therefore, whatever is dissolved must necessarily be dissolved according to the nature of those substances <note>The author argues that for a metal or mineral to become a liquid, it must first be chemically altered to resemble the nature of a salt or alum</note>. But because we see that all truly calcined <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to reduce it to a powder</term> materials are dissolved through the repetition of calcination and solution, we therefore prove by this that all calcined things approach the nature of salts or alums; thus, it is necessary that they share the same properties.

The method of solution is twofold: namely, by means of warm dung <note>original: "per fimum calidum"; decomposing horse manure was used as a consistent, low-heat source in early laboratories</note>, and by means of boiling water. These have one intention and one effect. 

The method by dung is as follows: let the calcined material be placed in a glass flask, and over it let there be poured a quantity of distilled vinegar, or something similar, double its amount. Let the top of the flask be well sealed so that it does not "breathe" <note>evaporate or leak</note>, and let it be left to dissolve in the lukewarm dung. Afterward, let the dissolved portion be removed by filtration. That which is not dissolved should be calcined again, and after calcination, let it be dissolved again in the same way, until by repeating the work upon it, the whole is dissolved. 

The method which is done by boiling water is faster. It is arranged so that the calcined material is placed in a flask with vinegar in the same way, with the opening sealed so it does not breathe. This flask is buried in a cauldron full of water and straw, just as we instructed in the order for the method of distillation by water <note>This describes a "Bain-marie" or water bath</note>. Afterward, let a fire be lit beneath it until the water boils for an hour. After this, let the dissolved part be distilled and kept aside. That which is not dissolved should be calcined again, and dissolved again in the same order, until through repetition the whole is dissolved.

# THE SUM OF PERFECTION BY GEBER

### Concerning Fixation, its causes, and the various ways of fixing bodies and spirits. Chapter 54.

**Fixation** <note>Latin: *Fixio*; the process of making a substance resistant to heat so it does not evaporate or "fly" from the fire.</note> is the suitable adaptation of a thing fleeing from fire so that it may endure the same. The reason for the invention of fixation is so that every tincture <note>The color-changing property of an alchemical elixir.</note> and every alteration may be made permanent in the thing altered, and not be changed. This process is diversified according to the variety of things to be fixed, which are namely certain bodies diminished from perfection, such as **Saturn** <note>Lead</note>, **Jupiter** <note>Tin</note>, **Mars** <note>Iron</note>, and **Venus** <note>Copper</note>. It also varies according to the diversity of the spirits themselves, which are namely **sulfur** and **arsenic** in one degree, and **quicksilver** <note>Mercury</note> in another; and in a third degree, **marcasite**, **magnesia**, and **tutia** <note>Zinc oxide or zinc ores</note>, and things similar to these.

Therefore, these bodies diminished from perfection are fixed by their **calcination** <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to reduce it to powder.</note>, because through it they are freed from their volatile and corrupting sulfurousness. We have spoken sufficiently of this in its own discourse, namely in the chapter on calcination.

However, **sulfur** and **arsenic** are fixed in two ways: namely, by the repetition of **sublimation** <note>The process where a solid turns into vapor and then back to solid, used here to purify and stabilize.</note> upon them in a vessel called an **aludel** <note>A pear-shaped chemical flask used in sublimation.</note>, until they remain stable. The intention for hastening their fixation is that you should strive to find a way to repeat the sublimation many times in a short time. This is done by using two aludels with their double covers in this order: namely, that you never cease from the act of sublimation until they have been fixed. Therefore, when they have ascended into one aludel, let them be cast into the other, and let it be done thus by alternating turns.

### FOURTH PART OF THE FIRST BOOK

### On Waxing. Chapter 55.

<note>The term "Ceration" (from the Latin *ceratio*) refers to a process of softening a substance until it has the consistency of wax, making it easier to melt or combine with other materials.</note>

Waxing is the softening of a hard, non-meltable substance until it reaches a state of liquefaction. From this, it is therefore clear that the reason for this invention was so that a substance—which previously could not penetrate a body because it lacked the ability to melt—might be softened for alteration so that it might flow and gain entry. For this reason, some have thought that waxing ought to be performed using liquid oils and waters. But that is an error, and entirely removed from the principles of this natural mastery <note>original: "magisterium naturale," referring to the Great Work of alchemy</note>, and is rejected by the manifest works of nature. For we do not see that nature has placed a moisture in metallic bodies that is quickly ended; rather, she has provided a long-lasting moisture for the necessity of their melting and softening. For if she had placed such a fleeting moisture in them, it would necessarily follow that by a single firing, the bodies would happen to be totally deprived of their moisture. Wherefore, it would follow from that, that after one firing, any body could neither be hammered nor melted. Therefore, imitating the works of nature as much as we can, it is necessary for us to follow nature’s method in waxing. Nature herself waxes at the very root of the waxing of meltable things by means of a moisture which stands above all other moistures, awaiting the heat of the fire. Therefore, it is also necessary and expedient for us to wax with a similar moisture. In no other things is this waxing moisture found better, more possibly, or more closely than in these, namely:

<note>The text breaks off here, likely to be continued with a list of specific substances on the following page.</note>

<summary>This chapter defines "ceration" as the process of softening hard minerals to a wax-like state to allow them to penetrate other metals. The author argues that this must be done using "permanent" moisture rather than common oils or water, imitating the natural composition of metals.</summary>

in sulfur and arsenic closely, but more closely and better in quicksilver <note>original: "argento uiuo"; literally "living silver," the historical term for mercury</note>. We do not see the humidity of these substances leave their earthy components because of the strong union they achieved in nature's process of mixing. However, in all other things that possess humidity, you will find by experiment that the moisture is separated from its earthy substance during dissolution, and after that separation, the substance is deprived of all humidity. In the aforementioned spirits <note>In alchemy, "spirits" refers to volatile substances like sulfur or mercury that can be vaporized</note>, however, this happens very little. Therefore, there is no other means by which we can be excused from using them in the process of waxing <term>Ceration: the process of softening a hard substance to a wax-like consistency</term>. But it seems better to me that their oils should first be fixed by means of oil of tartar <note>A solution of potassium carbonate, often used as a reagent</note>, and with those, every suitable and necessary waxing for this art should be performed.

### That the knowledge of the perfection of this art depends upon the knowledge of the nature of spirits and bodies, and that he wishes to treat copiously of both.
### Chapter 57.

It is truly not possible to know the transmutations of bodies, or of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"; mercury</note> itself, unless a true knowledge of their nature, according to their roots, comes upon the mind of the craftsman. Therefore, we shall first make known the principles of bodies—namely, what they are according to their causes, and what good or evil they contain within themselves. Afterward, we shall demonstrate the natures of all those bodies with all their properties—specifically, what the causes of their corruption are—proving these things with their own experiments.

### ## On the nature of the Sun, or Gold. Chapter 61.

**D**ealing now with the bodies, let us describe their innermost essence with a more expanded discourse. # SECOND PART OF THE SECOND BOOK

They are made in three ways: either through cleansing substances, or by the method of calcination <note>The process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its physical or chemical state, often reducing it to a powder.</note> and reduction <note>The chemical process of restoring a metal to its metallic state from an oxide or ore.</note>, or through solution.

Therefore, they are cleansed by purifying things in two ways: either reduced into lime <note>original: "calcem"; referring to the powdered oxide form of a metal</note>, or in their natural bodily state. Indeed, those reduced into lime are purified in this manner: either through salts, or through alums, or through glass. And it is done so that when the body has been calcined, then the water of alums or salts is poured over their lime, or glass is mixed with it, and it is reduced back into a body. This should be repeated over these bodies in alternating turns until they show themselves to be completely clean. For since salts, alums, and glass melt by a different fusion than the [metallic] bodies, they are therefore separated from them, and they carry the earthy substance away with them, leaving behind only the purity of the bodies.

In the natural state of the bodies, they are purified similarly and by the same method. And it is done by filing these two bodies <note>Likely referring to gold and silver, or the specific "diminished" metals mentioned later.</note> very finely; after this, they are treated with the same alums, salts, and glass, and afterwards reduced back into a body. And thus it should be repeated in alternating turns until they appear cleaner. They are also cleansed by a bath of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti uiui"; mercury</note>, the method of which we have already brought forward.

These bodies of both kinds are likewise cleansed through the repeated turn of calcination and reduction, with a sufficiency of their own fire, until they appear cleaner. For by this process, these diminished bodies are cleansed from perfection <note>The author suggests these metals are "imperfect" versions of gold or silver.</note>, away from a double corrupting substance: one which is indeed flammable and fleeting, and the other which is an earthy dross. ### On the Purification of Quicksilver. Chapter 73.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'I' depicting two figures, possibly scholars or alchemists, in a landscape with trees and foliage.</image-desc>
Therefore, from what has been previously stated, it is necessary to fully describe the purification of quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti uiui" (living silver), the common term for mercury.</note>. We say, therefore, that quicksilver is purified in two ways: either by sublimation <note>A process where a solid is heated until it turns into vapor and then solidifies again, leaving impurities behind.</note>, the method of which we have already brought forward; or by washing, the method of which is as follows. Let the quicksilver be poured into a glass or stone pan, and over it let a quantity of vinegar be poured, sufficient to cover it. Then, let it be placed over a slow fire and allowed to be heated just enough so that it can be handled with the fingers. Then, let it be stirred with the fingers until it is divided into the smallest parts, like a powder; and let it be stirred until all the vinegar that was poured into it is entirely consumed. Then, whatever earthiness <note>Impure, solid dross or residue.</note> is found in it should be washed with vinegar and cast away. Let this work be repeated upon it so many times until its earthiness is changed into a most perfect celestial color <note>Likely referring to a bright, sky-blue or shimmering silver sheen indicating purity.</note>, which is the sign of perfect washing. From these things, one must then proceed to the medicines.

# SECOND PART OF THE SECOND BOOK

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial letter 'A' featuring intricate foliate and scrollwork designs, set within a double-bordered square frame.</image-desc>

Let us therefore first bring forward a universal discourse concerning medicines <note>In alchemy, "medicine" refers to the elixir or agent used to transform base metals into noble ones</note>, along with their causes and manifest experiences. We suggest, therefore, that unless every superfluity is removed from imperfect bodies—whether by means of the medicine or through the method of preparation—they will not be perfected. Specifically, all superfluous sulfurous quality <note>original: "sulphureitas"; referring to the volatile, combustible principle in metals</note> and every unclean earthiness must be taken from them, so that they are not separated from the mixture during melting after the projection <note>The act of casting the medicinal powder onto the molten metal</note> of the altering medicine. When you have indeed discovered this, you already possess one of the distinct characteristics of perfection.

Similarly, unless the medicine also illuminates and alters the body into a white or lemon-yellow color <note>original: "citrinum"; the color associated with the transition to gold</note> according to the intention you seek—bringing forth a brilliance of luster and a pleasant clarity—the diminished bodies are not totally perfected in their completion. Furthermore, unless it specifically brings about a melting point like that of the Moon <note>silver</note> or the Sun <note>gold</note>, it is not changeable in its completion, because it does not remain stable under testing <note>original: "iudiciis"; literally "judgments" or assays</note>, but is entirely separated from the mixture and recedes. This, however, is demonstrated more extensively by us in the following pages in the chapter on the cupel <note>original: "cineritio"; a vessel used in the process of cupellation to refine precious metals</note>.

Furthermore, unless the medicine is made perpetual with a firm alteration of its impression, its change is of no value, for the impression does not remain but vanishes. Furthermore, unless it brings about the weights of perfection, it does not change under a firm and true completion of nature, in which there is no deception through the error of belief. For the weight of nature is one of the signs of perfection. It is clear, therefore, that since there are five distinct characteristics of perfection, it is necessary for the medicine of our mastery <note>original: "magisterij"; the Great Work or alchemical art</note> to bring these specific differences into the perfection.

It is necessary to investigate the density <note>original: "ponderis," referring to the specific gravity or "weight" which Alchemists believed indicated the purity of a metal</note> of the substances. We suggest, indeed, that it happens by necessity that there are three distinct orders of medicines. One is of the first order, another of the second, and another of the third.

I call a **medicine of the first order** any preparation of minerals which, when cast upon bodies that fall short of perfection, impresses an alteration upon them; yet this does not bring about a sufficient completion, for the altered metal may still change and be corrupted, with the total evaporation of the impression made by that medicine. An example of this is any whitening sublimation of **Venus** <note>Copper</note> or **Mars** <note>Iron</note> which has not undergone fixation <note>The process of making a volatile substance stable under heat</note>. Of this kind also is every addition of the color of **Sol** <note>Gold</note> and **Luna** <note>Silver</note>, or those mixed with Venus, placed over a cementing furnace, such as **verdigris** <note>original: "ziniar," a green pigment or acetate of copper</note> and similar things. For this changes the metal with a transformation that does not last, but rather diminishes itself through exhalation.

We call a **medicine of the second order** any preparation which, when cast upon bodies falling short of perfection, alters them in some specific quality of completion, yet leaves behind other qualities of corruption entirely. An example is the **calcination** <note>Reducing a metal to a powder or ash through heat</note> of bodies, by which every volatile element is deleted. To this class belongs the medicine that perpetually turns Luna <note>Silver</note> yellow <note>citrinans; to give it the appearance of gold</note>, or perpetually whitens Venus <note>Copper</note>, while leaving other corrupt qualities within them.

->Mercury<- <note>original: "argentum uiuum"</note> is sublimated <note>Sublimation is the process of heating a substance until it becomes vapor and then solidifies again, used here to purify the material.</note> so many times over the precipitated mercury, until the mercury is fixed in its own nature and provides a state of fusion. ### Concerning medicines that turn Silver yellow. Chapter 79.

Following the order of what has been previously established, we shall now describe with certain truth the medicine that colors the substance of Silver <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for Silver</note> yellow, according to the first class of medicines. This is a medicine which adheres to the Silver in its very depths, and by adhering, colors it—whether through its own natural properties or through the artifice of this mastery <note>the "mastery" refers to the alchemical art</note>. We will first describe the medicine that adheres to it by its own innate root, and then the artificial methods by which we make a substance of any kind adhere with a firm penetration.

We extract this medicine either from Sulfur, or from Quicksilver <note>original: "Argento uiuo," Mercury</note>, or from a mixture of both. However, it is extracted with less intensity through Sulfur, but more perfectly through Quicksilver. It is also extracted in a similar way through certain mineral substances which are not of this specific class, such as Vitriol and Copperas <note>iron or copper sulfates</note>, which is also called "gum of copper" or "drippings" of the same. 

We shall therefore present in the following sections all the methods for medicines that arise from Quicksilver; then those from Sulfur, or from a mixture of both; and finally, that which comes from the gum of copper or similar substances. 

The method for that which is made through Quicksilver is as follows: Take precipitate <note>mercury that has been processed into a solid form</note>, killed <note>chemically altered or "mortified" so it no longer flows</note> and fixed by precipitation. Then, let it be placed in a furnace of great heat, according to the method for preserving calxes <note>powders produced by heating metals</note> which we have taught, until it grows red like cinnabar <note>original: "usifur," a term for cinnabar or red mercuric sulfide</note>. If, however, it does not turn red, take a portion of Quicksilver that has not been killed...

Since the haste of melting <note>original: "liquefactionis festinantiam"; referring to metals that melt too quickly or unevenly</note> cannot be removed from the work, nor the impurity innate in the very root of its principles, it necessarily follows that we must seek a medicine. This medicine, when cast upon them, should thicken what is thin, and by thickening, harden it sufficiently to withstand the heat of melting. Conversely, it should thin the thickness in hard substances, and by thinning, bring them to a sufficient speed of fusion with the proper quality of ignition. It should also beautify the darkness of both types of bodies by cloaking them, transforming the one into white <note>silver</note> and the other into a most perfect yellow <note>gold</note>. This medicine does not differ from the medicine of the third order <note>the highest grade of the Philosopher's Stone</note> except by the imperfection of a lesser preparation. Nor does it differ within itself regarding its use on various bodies or the choice of pigments, but only in the method of its preparation. Similarly, the medicine for soft bodies requires one kind of industrious preparation to thicken their thinness, while the medicine for hard bodies requires another to thin their thickness. The latter requires the method of consuming fire, while the former requires the administration of preserving moisture.

### Concerning the Solar medicine of the third order. Chapter LXXXVI.

For the preparation of this Solar medicine <note>The "Solar medicine" refers to the Elixir or Philosopher's Stone capable of transmuting base metals into gold, which was associated with the Sun.</note>, let there be an addition of non-burning Sulfur <note>original: "Sulphuris non adurentis"; in alchemy, this refers to a purified, stable form of sulfur that does not vaporize or burn away easily.</note>, by way of fixing and calcining <term>calcination: the process of reducing a substance to powder by heat</term>, administered perfectly with the industry of skill, and a manifold method of solution with much reiteration, until it becomes clean: these things being preceded by a perfect administration, which is completed through sublimation <term>sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again, used for purification</term>. And the method of this addition is through the reiteration of the sublimation of the non-fixed part of the stone, with the ingenuity of joining them until it is elevated with it, and again fixed with it so that it remains stable. And the more the order of this exuberant completion is reiterated, the more the exuberance of this medicine is multiplied, its quality is further increased, and the growth of its perfection is greatly multiplied. 

And indeed, lest we be bitten by the impious <note>A common alchemical trope where the author claims to speak in riddles or brevity to prevent the "unworthy" from discovering the secret.</note>, we relate the entire completion of this mastery under a brief, complete, and known discourse. And its intention is that, through the method of sublimation, the stone and its addition may be most perfectly cleansed: and from here, by way of ingenuity, the volatile part of them may be fixed. Then, indeed, let the fixed be made volatile, and again the volatile be made fixed. And in this order is completed the most precious secret <note>original: "arcanum"</note>, which is above every secret of the sciences of this world, and an incomparable treasure. And you should exercise yourself toward it with the greatest instance of labor, and with the duration of immense meditation.

We shall investigate the differences in substance and the causes regarding the cupellation <note>original: "cineritij" – a process of refining gold or silver by heating it in a shallow vessel called a cupel, which absorbs base metals</note>, specifically why some things endure longer and others less so in the trial of this mastery <note>original: "magisterij" – the alchemical art or process</note> among those things diminished from perfection. However, we have sufficiently described the secret of these two bodies <note>likely referring to gold and silver</note> in the depths of their substance. And it is this: that their primary root was a great quantity of Quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti uiui" – Mercury</note>, and its essence was most pure and very subtle at first, but later thickened until it could undergo melting through ignition.

Therefore, whichever things diminished from perfection possess more earthiness <note>original: "terreitatis" – the presence of "earthy" impurities</note>, the less they endure in this trial; but whichever possess less, endure more. This is because these latter adhere more strongly due to the subtlety of their parts, which mix and unite themselves to the highest degree. Similarly, those bodies that are of greater thinness, or conversely, those bodies of greater density than those which stand in perfection, must necessarily be separated entirely from the mixture because they are not of the same melting point, and therefore they are separated. 

Indeed, those things participating in a smaller quantity of Quicksilver are more easily separated from the mixture. It is clear, then, that since Saturn <note>the alchemical name for Lead</note> is of much earthiness and of a small quantity of Quicksilver, and of an easy thinness of liquefaction—qualities which are most opposed to the perfection of the cupellation trial—it therefore endures the least among the other bodies in the mixture during the craft of cupellation; rather, it is separated and yields most quickly. And for that reason, since it yields more than the other bodies diminished from perfection, it is by this very fact more suited to the trial of this mastery, and that is because,

### The examination of the ash-cupel: how it should be composed and performed. Chapter 89.

<note>The woodcut initial 'N' depicts a figure resting in a landscape, symbolizing the observer or the alchemist in nature.</note> Let us therefore describe the method for this. Once it is melted, let us cast portions of **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnus" — the alchemical name for Lead</note> into it, one after another, and let it be blown upon with a flame of strong ignition. ### How the test of the Cement is to be composed and performed. Chapter 91.

Let us therefore describe the method of the Cement. Since it is known to us to be greatly necessary in the examination of perfection, we say that its composition is made with inflammable things. ### On Fusion. Chapter 94.

<note>The decorative initial 'I' depicts a scholar at his desk, symbolizing the studious application required for the alchemical art.</note>

In the account of fusion <note>original: "fusio," referring to the melting or smelting of metals</note>, let us provide a sufficient explanation according to the examination of all bodies and their specific ignition <note>original: "ignitio," the process of heating a substance until it glows</note>. We say, therefore, that there is only one fusion of perfection involving ignition, but not with just any kind of heating. It must be an ignition in which the body does not turn entirely white, and one in which no darkness <note>original: "fuscedo"</note> occurs when the fire is applied, and in which the body does not suddenly melt and liquefy so that it flows immediately after ignition. 

Therefore, when a body melts from the slightest pressure of a weak fire, either without glowing or with a dark glow, it is necessary that this body be of an imperfect preparation; each of the imperfect bodies belongs to a diminished craft <note>original: "artificio diminuto," implying a lower state of chemical refinement</note>. And if, after fusion, it is left to cool and its glow turns entirely and suddenly into blackness—and for this reason it loses its glow before it hardens—that body is not in a state of completion, regardless of what kind it may be. Rather, it is appropriate to judge this body as belonging to the soft varieties among the imperfect types of bodies. 

And if, indeed, with the laborious application of a strong and violent fire, its ignition occurs before fusion with a radiance of inestimable, entirely white brightness, the body has been altered not toward perfection, but toward hardness <note>original: "duritiei"</note>. ### On Calcination and Reduction. Chapter 97.

Next, we must investigate the examination of repeated calcination <term>calcination: the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to oxidize it or turn it into a powder</term> and reduction <term>reduction: the process of restoring a metallic powder or ore back to its solid metallic state</term>. We suggest, therefore, that the bodies of perfection <note>referring to gold and silver</note> are discovered through the repetition of calcination and reduction; by the differences in their quality, they lose nothing of their color, weight, or quantity (of which one should be very careful), nor any of their brilliance, no matter how many times the multiplicity of those operations is repeated upon them. And therefore, if through the repetition of the methods of calcination and reduction from the powder, any kind of altered metals should lose anything in their quality, you should consider that the craftsman has pursued a deceptive <note>original: "sophistice"; referring to "sophistical" or false alchemy</note> investigation. For this reason, you should practice these methods so that you may know them.

Therefore, let the son of doctrine <note>A traditional alchemical term for a dedicated student or initiate</note> not despair, because if he seeks it, he shall find it: not by doctrine alone, but by the investigation of his own natural movement. For he who seeks through the goodness of his own industry shall find knowledge. But he who seeks only through the pursuit of books shall arrive most slowly at this most precious art. For we have published this most true and entirely certain art, investigated by ourselves, for ourselves alone, and not for others. Therefore, we have enticed only the wise to the art, and through the ingenuity handed down by us, we have exposed the way of investigation to them. However, we have not written that it has been found except by ourselves alone, but we have written both the method of discovery and the ingenuity of those methods.

Common salt <note>Sodium chloride</note> should be dissolved in clear spring water, distilled through a filter, and congealed <note>evaporated to crystals</note> in an earthen vessel, or one of lead, or another metal. Saltpeter <note>Potassium nitrate</note> is dissolved in spring water and distilled through a filter; let it be congealed in a glass vessel until it reaches a crystalline fusion. Rock salt <note>Sal gemmae</note> is dissolved as before and congealed in a glazed earthen vessel. # GEBER ON THE DISCOVERY OF PERFECTION

It is expedient to investigate the nature of vitriols <note>original: "atramentorum"; literally "inks," but in this context referring to the family of sulfate minerals like green or blue vitriol</note>, since the knowledge we gather through them is very necessary for the tinting and binding of spirits <note>volatile substances like mercury or sulfur</note>, and other matters pertaining to that work. Black vitriol is dissolved in boiling water, distilled through a filter, and congealed; then it is ready for use. Copperas <note>ferrous sulfate</note> must be dissolved in distilled vinegar, clarified through a filter, and congealed, and thus it is purified. Roman vitriol <note>blue copper sulfate</note> requires no other preparation, except that in some cases it is held over a moderate fire until it turns red. Furthermore, it is certain that from imperfect bodies <note>base metals like lead or tin</note> are extracted dense substances necessary to us, which serve as aids to perfection in specific cases; these require preparation, and first we speak of white lead <note>original: "Cerussa plumbi"</note>. White lead is to be diluted in distilled vinegar, then purified of its coarser parts, and that which flows out like milk is to be congealed in the Sun or by a slow fire, and then it is prepared. Concerning Spanish white, tin-white, and minium <note>red lead</note>, the process is the same; for they are to be diluted in distilled urine and prepared in the same manner as white lead, and then they are prepared. Verdigris <note>original: "Viride aeris"; green of copper</note> should be dissolved in distilled vinegar, and once it has become a clear red <note>likely referring to the acetate solution</note>, it must be congealed by the slowest heat of a fire, and it is then prepared and ready. Saffron of iron <note>original: "Crocus ferri"; iron oxide</note> is to be dissolved in distilled vinegar and clarified; this reddish water of the saffron, once congealed, gives you the ready Saffron. Burnt copper <note>original: "Aes ustum"</note>, ground and washed with distilled vinegar according to the method we suggested for the preparation of white lead, will serve you well. Litharge <note>original: "Litargirium"; lead monoxide</note> dissolved in distilled vinegar should be clarified and congealed, for it is then well prepared; which again, just as the other things previously—

In the first part, we have treated sufficiently those things which seemed necessary to us in our certain discovery for the preparation of spirits and imperfect bodies. <image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'S' with floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>Grind native sulfur <note>original: "Sulphur uiuū"; literally 'living sulfur,' referring to naturally occurring, unrefined sulfur</note>, clear and gummy, very finely, and cook it in a lye made from potash <note>original: "cineribus clauellatis"; literally 'clubbed ashes,' a source of potassium carbonate</note> and quicklime. When this is done, remove it and stir with a rod; carefully draw off that which has come out with the lye, leaving the coarser parts at the bottom. Let that which was extracted cool slightly, and add to it a fourth part of good vinegar, and behold, the whole will congeal like milk. Draw off the clear lye as much as you are able; dry the residue over a slow fire and save it. For the second administration, follow this method: For one pound of this prepared sulfur, take one pound of iron scales <note>original: "squamis ferri"; the flaky byproduct of forging iron</note> well-calcined until red, one pound of well-calcined rock alum, and half a pound of prepared common salt. Incorporate all of this by grinding well with vinegar until it is liquid. Cook this, stirring until the whole has been well blackened, then dry it and grind it thoroughly. Place it in an aludel <term>aludel: a pear-shaped earthenware pot used as a condenser in the sublimation process</term> with a wide cover. Let the cover of the alembic <term>alembic: the cap or "still-head" used to direct vapors into a receiver</term> have a large and wide rim to preserve the rising of the spirits. Let the aludel be one and a half feet in height, so that the heat of the fire does not reach the rim of the alembic, and sublime it in this way, as we have taught in our *Sum of Perfection* <note>original: "summa perfectionis nostræ"; a reference to Geber's most famous work, the Summa perfectionis magisterii</note>. Its companion, Arsenic, after being ground down, must be boiled in vinegar, and in that same place all the combustible fatness <note>original: "pinguedo"; refers to oily impurities believed to hinder chemical transformation</note> is to be extracted and dried out. ### On the Preparation of Marcasite. Chapter 9.

Let crushed <term>Marcasite</term> <note>A metallic mineral, often iron pyrite or "fool's gold," used in alchemy to seek the essence of metals.</note> be placed in an <term>aludel</term> <note>A pear-shaped earthenware pot used as a condenser in the sublimation process.</note> with a wide base to the thickness of a finger. ### On the Preparation of Tutty. Chapter 10.

Powdered <term>Tutty</term> <note>A zinc oxide byproduct from smelting, used for medicinal and alchemical purposes.</note> is sublimated and made good by being placed in an aludel under the administration of great heat. <term>Sal ammoniac</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, a volatile salt used as a flux.</note> is sublimated from common salt, as we wrote to you in the practical manual on salts. <term>Quicksilver</term> is sublimated into a deep red state in this way: Take one pound of Mercury, two pounds of reddened <term>Vitriol</term> <note>Iron or copper sulfate, often used for its acidic properties.</note>, and one pound of <term>Saltpeter</term> <note>Potassium nitrate, a powerful oxidizing agent.</note> killed <note>In alchemy, to "kill" a substance means to change its physical state or neutralize its metallic "life" so it can be transformed.</note> together. Sublimate it also from calcined <term>alum of rocca</term> <note>A high-quality potassium alum.</note> and saltpeter with the same weights. 

And it is a great secret of our discovery that the dregs must be sent before; indeed, the consideration of the dregs must be noted in the sublimation of Sulphur and its companion <note>Likely referring to Arsenic, often considered the "partner" to Sulphur in alchemical theory.</note>. For Sulphur sublimated from the <term>calx</term> <note>The powdery residue left after a metal is burned or oxidized.</note> of copper is whitened more than from the calx of iron. And thus it must be investigated concerning <term>Arsenic</term>, for it is sublimated more red from iron. They can also be sublimated from Vitriol and calcined alum, and with common salt and saltpeter.

### On the preparation of Mars. Chapter XIV.

Prepare Mars <note>original: "Martem"; the alchemical term for Iron</note> in this way: Grind one pound of its filings with a half-pound of sublimated Arsenic. Moisten it with water of Saltpeter and alkali, repeating this three times; melt it with great heat, and you will have a white iron. Repeat the process until it melts sufficiently, with a singular whiteness.

Grind it three or four times, and reduce it <note>In alchemy, "reduction" refers to returning a calcined or powdered substance back to its solid metallic state</note> with saltpeter <note>potassium nitrate</note> and oil of tartar <note>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note>. For here we set down the practice step-by-step, while there we set down the theory of our speculation in a more general manner, organized with clear demonstrations.

# THE TRUTH OR PERFECTION.

## THE FOURTH PART
### of this book on medicines. Chapter 16.

Following the order of the preceding sections, we shall put into practice in this fourth part of ours the method of investigating how to compose any medicine—namely the white and the red—according to the nature and property of the body to be transmuted, or of Mercury itself with all its hidden and manifest characteristics. And in the second or third order, this book of ours accepts nothing false or deceptive <note>original: "sophisticum"</note>, since it is entitled "On the Discovery of Truth." For this reason, we shall begin first with the white Elixirs.

### On the Solar Medicine of the Third Order. Chapter XXII.

Son of doctrine, seek out experiments and do not cease, for you shall find a thousandfold fruit in them; for I have written this book for you alone, which I wish to complete with certain waters and oils that are very necessary in our mastery <note>The "mastery" or magisterium refers to the successful completion of the alchemical process</note>, for with these we shall seal our book concerning the discovery of perfection. And first, with our dissolving water <note>original: "aqua nostra dissolutiua"</note>, of which we made mention in our *Summa* when we spoke of Dissolution with the sharpness of waters. First, take one pound of Vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfate</note> of Copper, and a half-pound of Saltpeter <note>Potassium nitrate</note>, and one quarter of alum of Yemen <note>A high-quality grade of alum used as a mordant and astringent</note>; extract the water with the redness of the alembic <note>A reference to the distilling vessel and the color of the vapors or residue</note>. For it is greatly dissolving, and use it in the chapters mentioned before: it becomes much sharper, however, if you dissolve in it a quarter of Salt Ammoniac <note>Ammonium chloride</note>, because it then dissolves the Sun <note>Gold</note>, Sulfur, and Silver. Another philosophical water of ours for waxing <note>original: "inceratiua," referring to the process of bringing a substance to a soft, waxy consistency</note>. Take oil distilled from the whites of eggs, grind it with half as much Saltpeter and Salt Ammoniac, in equal parts, and it is made very well; or mix it with Alkali Salt and distill as before, and the more you repeat this, the better it waxes. Or, join the aforesaid oil with oil of Tartar <note>Potassium carbonate solution</note> and distill a white waxing oil. Red waxing oil: Take oil of egg yolks, or of human hair, to which add as much Salt Ammoniac, and distill again, and do this three times, and it will be a very red waxing oil. Oil...

# GEBER ON DISCOVERY

Oil of verdigris <note>original: "uiridis æris"; a green pigment or crust formed on copper, often used in alchemy as a base for tinctures</note> is made when verdigris is dissolved in water of sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>; and with that mixture congealed, mix in oil of egg yolks and distill it. By repeating this process three times, you will have oil of verdigris, which is suitable and useful for the process of softening solids with oil <term>inceration</term>.

Oil of gall is made by extracting the oil from bile, just as one does with human hair, performing the process in all respects as with other substances. And I do not say that these substances provide a fundamental mineral moisture <note>radical moisture was believed to be the life-sustaining fluid within matter</note>, as we have demonstrated regarding Sulfur and Arsenic; rather, they protect the tincture from being consumed by fire until it penetrates the metal, and afterwards they escape when the heat is applied, as has been recounted by us elsewhere.

Whosoever the craftsman may be who, according to our instructions delivered in this book of ours, shall have worked perfectly and studiously, he shall find after the completion of his work that we have investigated the truth. And with this, our book is finished, which is titled *On the Discovery of Truth or Perfection*.

# THE BOOK OF FURNACES by Geber the Arab, most skillful philosopher and expert in natural matters, pertaining to the practice of <term>alchemy</term> <note>original: "χυμείαν" (khumeian); the art of transmuting and purifying metals</note>, translated by Rodogerus of Seville.

## Preface, dividing the book into three parts. Chapter I.

<image-desc>An ornate woodcut initial 'C' featuring a detailed landscape illustration within its frame, depicting a seated figure or shepherd in a pastoral setting with trees and a building in the distance.</image-desc>

We have considered, with a consideration that is not based on fantasy, that we have handed down the entire art within our volumes. However, lest we be bitten by the envy of others, we have set forth this Book of Furnaces, in which we shall treat manual practice, regarding the preparations of both spirits <note>volatile substances like sulfur or mercury</note> and bodies <note>solid metals</note>, so that craftsmen may more easily reach the completion of the work. Since, therefore, the final consideration consists in the knowledge of things more closely related, and in the method of operating, and since things can be extracted from other things by the governance of fire; and since we cannot arrive at this goal except by separating the superfluous from the desired content—namely, the combustibility of sulfur and the earthiness that defiles any body—it is for this reason that we shall first treat the individual modes of operating. For instance, we shall discuss what kind of furnace with its instruments is suited for preparing any given thing, up to the completion of the work with the governance of fire appropriate to it, and what kind of vessels pertain to the purpose.

so that the craftsman may be able to complete his work. Second, we shall discuss which things must be prepared so that he may be able to generate true Gold <note>original: "Solem" (the Sun), the alchemical symbol for gold</note> or Silver <note>original: "Lunam" (the Moon), the alchemical symbol for silver</note> with brilliance from simple or mixed substances. Third, we shall describe those things which can be accomplished with altering agents, and those which are naturally altered with total completion; also the method of mixing with due proportion, and with medicines <note>In alchemy, a "medicine" refers to a substance or elixir used to transform base metals into noble ones</note> prepared over a long time for these purposes. At the end, however, we shall provide a recapitulation of all our experiments, through which we arrived at the knowledge of this truth.

# THE FIRST PART OF THIS
## book on the methods of operating.
### Concerning the calcining furnace. Chapter 11.

Let a square calcining furnace <note>A furnace used for calcination, the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its physical or chemical state</note> be made, four feet in length and three feet in width, and let the thickness of the walls be half a foot in this manner. Therefore, let Silver, Copper <note>original: "Venus"</note>, Iron <note>original: "Mars"</note>, or other things to be calcined be placed in earthen pans made of the strongest clay—the kind from which crucibles are made—so that they may be able to withstand the harshness of the fire until the total combustion of calcination is achieved. Calcination is the treasure of the matter; do not let the work of calcination weary you. Study closely what we have said in our volumes. Through calcination, imperfect bodies are purified, and also through the reduction of the calcined material back into a solid mass. And then let our medicine be projected <note>The act of "projection" involves casting the transformative elixir onto the molten metal</note> upon them, and rejoice.

In the <term>sublimation</term> <note>The process of heating a solid substance until it turns into vapor and then collects again as a solid on a cooler surface</note> of sulfur, you must construct the cover of the sublimator with a large, unobstructed concave channel on the inside, fashioned in the manner of an <term>alembic</term> <note>A hooded chemical vessel used for distilling</note> but without a "nose" or spout. For otherwise, the entire sublimated material would fall back down to the bottom of the vessel due to excessive heat. Indeed, at the end of the sublimation process, the sulfur does not ascend except by force of pressure, continuing until the <term>aludel</term> <note>A pear-shaped earthenware pot used as a condenser in the sublimation process</note> reaches a state of glowing heat. Unless the sublimated material were held in that upper channel—since it melts quite easily—it would flow back down the sides of the vessel to the very bottom, and thus nothing would be found to have been sublimated, as is well known to those experienced in this art.

## On the descensory furnace. Chapter 5.

The descensory furnace <note>A "descensory" furnace is designed so that the melted material flows downward through a filter or grate into a receiver below, preventing it from staying in contact with the heat for too long.</note> is constructed in this manner.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a descensory furnace and its parts. On the left, a funnel-shaped vessel is shown with a flat, grated or perforated top; above it is a circular lid. And it is wonderfully common among us, specifically among the smelters of ash-ores <note>original: "cineritiorum" — likely referring to the remains of cupellation or ores processed with ash</note> and cements <note>original: "cementorum" — in alchemy, "cementing" refers to a process of purifying gold or silver by heating it with powdered minerals</note>. Furthermore, all bodies that have been calcined <note>reduced to powder by heat</note>, burnt, dissolved, and coagulated are reduced back into a solid mass by means of this furnace. Indeed, it is used for the ash-ores, cements, and the shells or crucibles in which silver has been frequently melted, in order to recover that metal which has been absorbed into them.

### Concerning the Melting Furnace. Chapter VI.

The melting furnace <note>original: "furnus fusorius"</note> is one in which all bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the seven known metals: gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, and mercury.</note> are easily melted by themselves. ### On the Calcination of Jupiter. Chapter 10.

Jupiter <note>term: Jupiter (tin)</note> is specifically calcined <note>term: calcination (reducing a metal to a powder or oxide through heat)</note> in this way: Let there be a large earthen vessel situated over the furnace, and once the tin is placed within, add an equal amount of prepared common salt and calcined rock alum. ### On the Calcination of Venus <note>original: "Veneris"; refers to Copper</note>. Chapter XII.

*Venus is calcined in this manner: It is placed in the aforementioned furnace of calcination, either in the form of filings, or by itself, or with powdered arsenic, or with sulfur, being anointed with common oil. And thus it is calcined for three or four days with a very strong fire. Strike the calcined material so that it falls from the plates; calcine the remainder, and re-calcine that which has been calcined and ground until it is perfectly turned red, and preserve it.*

### On the Calcination of Mars <note>original: "Martis"; refers to Iron</note>. Chapter XIII.

*Mars is indeed calcined by means of its filings in the aforementioned furnace, until it has been perfectly turned red, like an impalpable powder that cannot be felt. And it is called Saffron of Mars <note>original: "crocus Martis"; a term for iron oxide used as a pigment or medicine</note>.*

### On the calcination of intermediate minerals. Chapter XIIII.

*All vitriols <note>original: "atramenta"; literally 'blackings', referring to sulfate minerals</note>, salts, alums, and types of Tutty <note>original: "Thutiæ"; zinc oxide deposits from furnace chimneys</note> are calcined with tartar and various other substances in the said Calcining furnace, with a moderate or strong fire according to the requirement of the thing to be calcined, as is evident in the book "On the Investigation of the Perfect Mastery" <note>original: "De investigatione perfecti magisterii"; a famous alchemical treatise attributed to Geber</note>, but all bodies are calcined as described in our Testament.*

### On the washings of calxes <note>term: calx - the powdery residue left after a metal has been burned or oxidized</note> and burnt bodies. Chapter XV.

*The washing of all burnt and calcined bodies is done thus: First, have a glazed earthen vessel*

then, a large vessel filled with warm fresh water. ### On the Waxing of Washed Calxes. Chapter XVI.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'I' depicting two figures, likely alchemists or scholars, in an interior or landscape setting.</image-desc>The <term>incerations</term> <note>The process of softening a dry substance into a wax-like consistency, often by adding liquids.</note> of washed calxes are done as follows: Dry the washed calx, then dissolve in two pounds of distilled vinegar: common salt, <term>glacier alum</term> <note>Potassium alum, often found in clear, ice-like crystals.</note>, and <term>rock salt</term> <note>Pure crystalline halite.</note>, two ounces of each. Moisten four pounds of the aforementioned dried, washed calx until it has absorbed all the aforementioned liquid; dry it, and preserve it.

### On the Governance of Mercury. Chapter 24.

<margin>Refining Silver</margin>
Regarding the amalgamation of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"; the metal Quicksilver</note> and Moon <note>original: "Lunae"; the alchemical name for Silver</note>, place the remainder of the cement <note>a corrosive powder used in refining</note> on top, so that the globe sits in the middle of the cement. The Silver will then be much improved in weight, density <note>original: "surditate"; literally 'deafness,' referring to the dull sound of pure metal compared to the ring of alloys</note>, and stability <note>original: "fixione"; the ability to withstand heat without evaporating</note>.

**Also:** Amalgamate Silver with Mercury, to which you should add as much Saturn <note>original: "Saturni"; the alchemical name for Lead</note> as there is Silver. Place this in another crucible so that three-quarters of it remains empty. Pour oil of sulfur over it and cook it until the oil is consumed. Afterward, keep it for two hours in a moderate fire, and a black stone with a slight redness will be generated there. Pass this stone through the cupel, and you will find the Silver increased in weight, density, and stability.

**Another method to be considered:** Grind the Silver amalgamated with Mercury with twice its amount of metallic arsenic. To this, add a tenfold proportion of amalgamated Venus <note>original: "Veneris"; the alchemical name for Copper</note>—that is, ten times the amount of the Silver and arsenic combined. Grind the whole mixture, fix it <note>render it non-volatile</note>, and reduce it back into a solid body, and it will go well for you.

# THE MOST LEARNED
## MAN ROGER BACON’S
### LITTLE BOOK ON ALCHEMY, TO WHICH
### he gave the title, The Mirror of Alchemy.

->PREFACE.<-

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'M' featuring a youth or angel seated amidst scrolling foliage.</image-desc>
In many ways and in various fashions, the philosophers <note>The "philosophers" here refers to the ancient alchemists and natural scientists like Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus.</note> spoke of old through their writings, when, as if in a riddle and with a clouded voice, they left to us a certain science—noble above all others—entirely obscured and altogether denied under a veil of despair. And this they did not do without cause. Therefore, I command that, above all the writings of others, you firmly fix your mind upon these seven chapters containing within themselves the transformation of metals; revolve their beginning, middle, and end frequently in your heart, and you shall find in them such subtlety that your soul shall be fulfilled.

### On the natural principles and the procreations of minerals. Chapter II.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' at the beginning of the chapter, featuring floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

Secondly, I shall perfectly declare the natural principles and the procreations of minerals. # THE ALCHEMY OF ROGER BACON

...purity, or unclean superfluity, and from such a defect, receive these truths.

*On the nature of gold.* Gold is indeed a perfect body, generated from pure, fixed, clear, and red Quicksilver <note>original: "Argento uiuo"; mercury</note>, and from clean, fixed, red, and non-burning Sulfur; it possesses no defect.

*On the nature of Silver.* Silver is a clean, pure, and almost perfect body, created from pure, nearly fixed, clear, and white Quicksilver, and from such Sulfur; it lacks only a small amount of fixation, color, and weight.

*On the nature of Tin.* Tin is a clean but imperfect body, created from pure Quicksilver—partially fixed and partially not fixed—which is clear and white in its outward appearance but red in its hidden interior, and from such Sulfur; it lacks only further decoction or digestion <note>The alchemical process of "ripening" a metal through heat</note>.

*On the nature of Lead.* Lead is an unclean and imperfect body, created from impure, non-fixed, earthy, and dross-filled Quicksilver, which is somewhat white in appearance and red in its hidden interior, and from a Sulfur that is combustible in some part; it lacks purity, fixation, color, and the proper fire.

*On the nature of Copper.* Copper is an unclean and imperfect body, generated from impure, non-fixed, earthy, and burning Quicksilver that is a dull red, and from such Sulfur; it lacks fixation, purity, and weight, and it possesses too much impure color and non-burning earthiness.

*On the nature of Iron.* Iron is an unclean and imperfect body, generated from impure, excessively fixed, earthy, and burning Quicksilver that is a dull white and red, and from such Sulfur; it lacks the ability to melt easily <note>original: "fusio"</note>, purity, and weight. It possesses too much fixed, unclean sulfur and burning earthiness.

Every Alchemist ought to take note of these things just stated.

# THE MIRROR OF ALCHEMY

### Chapter III. From which substances the material of the elixir is most closely to be drawn.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap 'I' featuring two figures (likely putti) playing or struggling amidst floral ornamentation.</image-desc>

In what has already been said, the procreation of both perfect and imperfect metals has been sufficiently determined. Now let us return to the choosing and perfecting of the imperfect material. Since it is well enough known from the preceding chapters that all metals are procreated from Quicksilver <note>original: "Argento uiuo"; Mercury</note> and Sulfur, and how their impurity and uncleanness corrupts them; and since no thing ought to be applied to metals which is not composed of or descended from them, it is left clearly enough to us that no foreign thing, which did not take its origin from these two, is powerful or sufficient to perfect them, or to bring about a new transmutation of them. 

Wherefore it is a thing to be wondered at, that any prudent man should base his intention upon animals or vegetables, which are far removed <note>The author argues that biological materials like blood or plants are chemically unrelated to metals</note>, when minerals are found to be close enough. Nor is it to be believed at all that any of the philosophers placed the Art in the aforementioned remote things, except by way of metaphor. But from the two aforementioned substances all metals are made, and nothing adheres to them, nor is joined to them, nor transmutes them, except that which is from them. And so, by right, we must take Quicksilver and Sulfur as the material of our stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone"</note>. Neither Quicksilver by itself alone, nor Sulfur by itself alone, generates any metal, but from the diverse mixing of them both, [me-]

Metals are created in diverse ways, as are many minerals. Therefore, our chosen matter must consist of a mixture of both <note>The "both" refers to the dual principles of Mercury and Sulfur</note>. But our final secret is most excellent and deeply hidden: from which specific mineral thing should it be most closely and nearly prepared? We are bound to choose this with great care.

Suppose, then, that our matter were chosen first from **vegetables**, such as herbs, trees, or anything that grows from the earth. In that case, it would first be necessary to produce **Quick-silver** <note>original: "Argentum vivum"; Mercury</note> and **Sulfur** from them through long decoction <note>The process of boiling or heating to extract essence</note>. We are excused from this labor, however, because Nature already provides us with Quicksilver and Sulfur.

And if we were to choose from **animals**, such as human blood, hair, urine, excrement, chicken eggs, or anything proceeding from animals, it would likewise be necessary to produce Quicksilver and Sulfur from them by decoction; from which we are excused, as stated before.

If we were to choose from **intermediate minerals**, such as all kinds of **Magnesias** <note>A term used for various mineral ores, often pyrites or manganese</note>, **Marcasites** <note>Iron pyrites, often called "Fool's Gold"</note>, **Tutias** <note>Zinc oxide deposits from furnaces</note>, **Atraments** or **Vitriols** <note>Sulfate minerals used for making inks and acids</note>, **Alums**, **Borax** <note>original: "Baurach"</note>, **Salts**, and many others, it would similarly be necessary to produce Quicksilver and Sulfur from them by decoction, from which—as with the others—we are excused.

And if we were to choose any of the **seven spirits** <note>In alchemy, "spirits" are volatile substances that can be sublimated or evaporated</note> by itself—such as Quicksilver alone, or Sulfur alone, or Quicksilver with one of the two Sulfurs, either **living Sulfur** <note>Native or crude sulfur</note>, or **Orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum"; arsenic trisulfide, a yellow pigment</note>, or **yellow or red Arsenic** alone or paired—we would achieve nothing at all. For Nature never perfects anything without an equal mixture of both <note>Mercury and Sulfur</note>; nor can we, from whom then, as from the aforesaid...

# THE MIRROR OF ALCHEMY

We are excused from using <term>Quicksilver</term> <note>original: "Argento vivo," literally living silver or mercury</note> and Sulfur in their raw states. Ultimately, if we were to choose them exactly as they are, we would be required to mix them according to a proper proportion which human genius does not know, and afterwards to cook them until they coagulate into a solid mass. Therefore, we are excused from receiving both in their own natural forms—namely Quicksilver and Sulfur—since we are ignorant of the aforementioned proportion, and instead, we find bodies <note>referring to the "perfect" metals, gold and silver</note> in which we find these elements already proportioned, coagulated, and joined together in the proper manner. Keep this secret most secretly.

Gold is a perfect and masculine body, without any excess or deficiency. If it could perfect imperfect metals simply by being mixed with them in a state of melting, it would be the <term>Red Elixir</term> <note>the highest form of the Stone, capable of transmuting metals into gold</note>. Silver is also a nearly perfect and feminine body; if it could nearly perfect imperfect metals through common melting, it would be the <term>White Elixir</term> <note>the lesser Stone, which transmutes metals into silver</note>. But this is not the case, nor can it be, because they are only "simple" perfect bodies. If that perfection were merely mixable with the imperfect, the imperfect would not be perfected by the perfect; rather, the perfection of the perfect would be diminished and made imperfect by the presence of the imperfect. 

However, if they were "more than perfect"—whether by double, quadruple, a hundredfold, or more—then they could perfect the imperfect. And because nature always works simply, the perfection in them is simple, inseparable, and unmixable,

* nor could they be placed in the Stone as a <term>ferment</term> <note>a substance that "leavens" or triggers the transformation of the whole mass</note> by art to shorten the work, and then be reduced to their original state, since the total amount of the <term>volatile</term> <note>substances that evaporate or change easily</note> overcomes the total amount of the <term>fixed</term> <note>substances that resist fire and remain solid</note>.

In the mineral mountains, the thickness of the water is cooked and thickened to such an extent that, over time, it becomes quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the historical term for mercury</note>. God has given nature a linear path—namely, continuous cooking—and you fools either despise or are ignorant of how to imitate it.
