Regarding the law of nature, it is established as noteworthy to us that the external mineral mountain is everywhere closed within itself and stony; for if the heat were able to escape, metals would by no means be procreated. Therefore, if we intend to imitate nature, we must of necessity provide a furnace in such a manner, after the likeness of mountains—not in size, but in continuous heat—so that the fire placed within, when it ascends, finds no exit, and the heat reverberates against the vessel containing the material of the stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the goal of alchemical transformation.</note> within itself, firmly closed. This vessel ought to be round with a small neck, made of glass or of some earth representing the nature or density of glass, the mouth of which must be marked or sealed with such a cover and bitumen <note>A type of airtight sealant or "Lute of Hermes."</note>. And just as in the mines the heat does not immediately touch the matter of the Sulfur and Quicksilver <note>original: "Argenti uiui." In alchemy, Sulfur and Quicksilver/Mercury are the two primary principles of all metals.</note>, because the earth of the mountain is everywhere in between; so the fire ought not to touch the vessel containing the aforementioned matter immediately, but it is to be placed within another vessel, similarly closed, so that the tempered heat may reach the matter better and more aptly from above, below, and everywhere. Whence Aristotle says in the *Light of Lights* <note>original: "Lumine Luminum," a medieval alchemical text often attributed to Aristotle or Rhazes.</note> that Mercury is to be cooked in a triple vessel. And let the vessel be of the hardest glass, or, what is better, of earth possessing the nature of glass.

### Preface: How art imitates nature. Chapter I.

<image-desc>Large decorative initial letter 'C' containing a woodcut illustration of a figure, likely a philosopher or alchemist, seated at a desk or workbench in a room with a window.</image-desc> Since every improvement of things increases the nature of that specific thing to which it belongs, it follows that in many of the philosophers' teachings, nature is improved through <term>art</term> <note>In this context, "art" refers to alchemy or human skill acting upon the natural world.</note> beyond the movement it possessed in its original form. And yet, no thing can be worked upon except through the mediation of nature, since nature herself works secretly and intrinsically within the art through the administration of that art. From this it follows that the improvement of nature is an increase of its power, and the labor of art is the improvement of that thing. For nature completes its own degree—that which it is naturally able to complete—and it cannot surpass that limit unless nature herself is hindered by the interference of art. For although art does not transcend nature by creating a "new" nature through simple labor, art does transcend nature in regard to that specific nature which it can properly refine. And therefore it is said: Art imitates nature, not because it builds a new nature, but because it refines the power of that existing nature. To this end, art begins to make progress where nature...

Therefore every species, in its own species, and every genus in its own genus, and every nature in its own nature, naturally aims for the increase of its power, and brings forth fruit according to its own nature, and not in another nature contrary to itself; since everything sown corresponds to its own seed—we say this in regard to generation. # THE CORRECTOR
<note>original: "Correctorium" — likely referring to the "Correctorium Alchimiae," a text often attributed to Richardus Anglicus or other medieval alchemists, intended to "correct" the errors of practitioners.</note>

Every inferior thing working upon a matter strives to destroy the superior, and every superior thing working upon a matter strives to bring the inferior to perfection. And therefore, it is necessary for every craftsman to imitate nature, and to understand the nature of that thing which his art imitates; otherwise, he is foolishly seen to be "improving" nature through art without understanding it.

### That the study of philosophy is necessary for this art. Chapter II.

<image-desc>Historiated woodcut initial 'S' depicting a human figure entwined with floral patterns.</image-desc>
Study, according to the teachers, dispels ignorance and leads the human intellect back to true science and the knowledge of any given thing. Therefore, it is first necessary to acquire knowledge through the study of this sweet work, and to sharpen the wit through the sayings of the philosophers, since the way of truth is known within them. If, therefore, those who labor do not despise the work, they shall sweetly taste the fruit proceeding from it. But those who shrink from study should weigh carefully in their thoughts while working whether their art is truly an imitation of nature—especially of that thing whose nature their art is supposed to improve. For without the imitation of nature, it is impossible for them to bring the secrets of the philosophers to a perfect conclusion. As the philosopher says of such people: they pass into practice just like a donkey goes to hay, not knowing why he stretches out his snout, except insofar as his external senses, without intellect, lead him to his fodder through sight and taste. So these "donkeys" without true principles and fruitful studies...

### What the parts of minerals are. Chapter 4.

Mineral bodies <note>original: "corpora mineralia"</note> are specifically distinguished into two parts: namely, into the metallic part—that is, into the metals which derive their origin from Mercury <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the principle of fluidity and metallic luster, not just the liquid metal we know today.</note>, such as Gold, Silver, Copper, Tin, Lead, and Iron—and these are called the major minerals. And into the mineral part, which does not derive its origin from Mercury, such as salts, black inks <note>original: "atramenta," likely referring to vitriol or ferrous sulfates used in making ink</note>, alums, vitriol, arsenic, orpiment <note>a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, sulfur, and the like; and these are called the minor minerals, yet they are non-metallic bodies. Since it is manifest that the major minerals—that is, the metallic bodies—have their origin from sulfur and Quicksilver <note>original: "Argento uiuo"</note>, according to whether they are more or less purified. And now I shall set down the difference of their generation, and I shall say from whence they have their origin, which nevertheless is sufficiently clear in many books of the philosophers.

### Concerning metals, which derive their origin from Mercury in general. Chapter 5.

All liquefiable metals which derive their origin from Mercury are ductile <note>capable of being hammered thin or drawn into wire</note>. For their matter is a watery substance, mixed with an earthy substance by a strong commixture, and one cannot be separated from the other; wherefore the watery substance of it is congealed with great cold after

### How metals are made specifically from Mercury. Chapter VI.

The nature of all liquefiable things is naturally produced from Mercury, or quicksilver <note>original: "Argento uiuo"</note>, and the substance of its own sulphur, because it is the property of quicksilver to be coagulated by a vapor, or by the heat of white or red sulphur that is non-burning. ### That it is impossible for intermediate minerals to be artificially made into metals. Chapter 10.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' inside a square frame, featuring elaborate foliate and scrolling vine designs.</image-desc>
But because it was determined in the preceding chapter that lesser minerals cannot be artificially made into metals, it remains to prove this more strongly for the sake of greater truth. First, in this way: Because lesser minerals are not generated from the <term>prime matter</term> <note>The fundamental substance from which all things are thought to originate</note> of metals, which is Mercury. Since, however, their generation differs from the generation of Mercury in the first place—in form, in matter, and in composition—therefore they also cannot become metals. For of one species there is one prime matter and <term>seed</term> <note>original: "sperma"; used here in the biological sense of a generative starting point</note> from which it is generated. But the first part of the preceding statement is clear, because lesser minerals are not generated from Mercury, as is evident through Aristotle and Avicenna <note>Ibn Sina, a Persian polymath whose medical and alchemical theories were foundational in the Middle Ages</note>. Therefore, if they were to become metals, it would be necessary that they first pass into the prime matter of metals. But because this cannot be done artificially, they will by no means become metals. Thus the second part of the preceding statement is sufficiently clear, as was declared in the preceding chapter. Secondly, to the same point: Because lesser minerals cannot be made into the beginning of the art <note>the alchemical process</note> artificially, which is Mercury, therefore they also do not reach the middle and the end, which are metal and <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tictura"; the transformative substance or elixir sought by alchemists</note>. The logic holds: Because nourishment in a human cannot become a human through generation unless it is first converted into seed, and thus, with its like added, a new human is generated. But because lesser minerals are of a foreign nature to metals...

### On the difference between common sulfur and the simple, non-burning sulfur of the philosophers. Chapter 11.

<image-desc>Ornate square woodcut initial 'N' decorated with acanthus leaf motifs.</image-desc>

Now we must inquire concerning the difference between the simple sulfur of the philosophers, which does not burn, and common sulfur. Since the philosopher <note>Likely referring to Aristotle or Geber, the traditional authorities in alchemy.</note> speaks generally, saying: "Sulfur coagulates Mercury," we must ask: Does every kind of sulfur coagulate Mercury? It must be said that it does not. For every type of common sulfur, according to the philosopher, is contrary to metals. Likewise, Avicenna <note>original: "Auicenna"; the influential Persian polymath whose works formed the basis of medieval alchemy.</note> says: It does not enter into our mastery <term>Mastery: The "Magisterium" or the successful completion of the Great Work</term>, because it did not originate from it; it always infects, blackens, and corrupts, in whatever way it may be prepared by artifice. For it is itself an infected fire. Therefore, if it is fixed <note>original: "figitur"; rendered solid or non-volatile</note>, it hinders melting, nor is it impossible for it to be joined to a body. An example of this is seen in iron, which is known to have fixed, coarse, and unclean sulfur within itself. # RICHARD THE ENGLISHMAN

Just as ice is not dissolved into water by heat, it does not join with the water in which it lies, nor does it tint that water with its own power—which was previously congealed within it from the nature of its species. Thus, in the same way, if you do not dissolve the body into **Mercury** by means of Mercury, you cannot obtain the hidden power from it—namely, the sulfur which has been digested and ripened by the work of nature within the mineral. Thus the stone is one, a single medicine, which according to the philosophers is called **Rebis** <note>From the Latin "res bina," meaning a double thing or a thing composed of two parts.</note>, that is, made from a twofold thing: specifically from a body and a spirit, whether white or red. In this matter many fools have erred, interpreting it in various ways:

> The **Rebis** is the most upright rule in the described figures.

That is to say, two things; and these two things are one thing—namely, the water joined to the body, by which the body is dissolved into spirit, which is to say, into the **Mineral water** from which it was made from the beginning. And so from the body and the spirit, one Mineral water is made, which is called the **elixir**, that is, the **ferment** <term>fermentum: a substance that acts like leaven, transforming the whole mass into its own nature</term>, because then the water and the spirit are one single thing. From this is made the tincture and the medicine for purging all bodies, which seems impossible to many fools. Therefore, from one thing, which is the water of the body and the spirit, the medicine is perfected. Whence the verses:

> This art deceives many fools through its riddles.
> The Art nourishes one thing, which anyone knows well.
> Many desire this thing, yet the thing is but one.
> Nothing is like it, and it is also cheap in price.
> Nor should it be despised, for it performs stupendous feats.
> You must fix this thing, and tame it in the fire.

# RICHARD THE ENGLISHMAN

## How white and red sulfur exist in the Moon and the Sun. Chapter XII.

Since it has been said that the red sulfur of the philosophers <note>original: "sulphur philosophorum"; a metaphorical substance representing the active, masculine, or "fiery" principle in alchemy, not common brimstone</note> exists in the Sun through greater digestion, and white sulfur exists in the Moon through lesser digestion. * Whence the philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus, often cited as "The Philosopher" in medieval texts</note> says: Yellowing is nothing other than complete digestion. For heat acting upon the moist first generates blackness, and acting upon the dry, it generates whiteness; when the fire transcends this whiteness, acting within it, it causes a most pure yellowness. And all these things can be observed in the calcination <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to achieve oxidation or reduction to powder</note> of lead. 

The philosopher also says that each of the perfect bodies <note>gold and silver</note> already contains its own good sulfur in actuality along with Mercury: namely, gold contains golden sulfur, and silver contains silvery sulfur. Therefore, white sulfur becomes golden through yellowing, because red sulfur—that is, the substance of fire—is present there, which has digested this white sulfur further; and thus both white and red sulfur exist on both sides within the Sun. For this reason, fire is its highest perfection, as things generated in fire. And therefore, nature amicably rejoices in its own fiery nature. 

Whence it is asked: Can any foreign things cause this in the bodies? Since art <note>alchemy</note> is nothing else, through the mediation of nature, but the cooking and digestion of that nature through simple labor. For example: In the morning when I have risen and I see my urine is white, I judge that I have slept too little; I therefore lay myself back down to sleep, and having taken sleep, the urine becomes yellow; and this happens in no other way except through the digestion of the natural heat existing within me. So follow nature through art in a similar way by cooking...

# THE REFORMER

By cooking, digesting, maturing, and refining—since nature already contains within itself a natural fire by which things are ripened—this is something other substances do not possess, and therefore they cannot bestow it. In Moon <note>original: "Luna," the alchemical name for Silver</note>, however, there is nothing but a simple white sulfur, not as fully digested as the red sulfur, since it has not been deprived of its blackness through the action of the heat which it naturally contains within itself. Rather, it is a hidden and concealed species of fire, acting both in art <note>meaning alchemy or human skill</note> and in nature, and vice versa. And therefore, it is not impossible that art, with nature as its mediator, may digest and perfect this further, since nature naturally desires to reach perfection; yet nature cannot achieve this on its own unless it is assisted by art and practical operation. However, these labors, as I believe, do not reach the man of "stiff neck" <note>a biblical idiom for the stubborn or arrogant</note>, because good workers are rarely found. And for this reason, true Silver and Gold are not produced unless they are so digested and boiled—or used as a medicine <note>the "Elixir" or "Tincture"</note>—with which the inferior substance is tinted and improved for the better. For the intention of all philosophers is to perfect the inferior with the superior. Fools, conversely, understand this the wrong way, because they strive to perfect the superior with the inferior; they seek a thing in a substance where it never existed, namely Gold and Silver in dross and combustible things. They do this through sophistry so that they might appear true to men, as was said before.

Can it be drawn out? I say that it cannot. For it was said previously that in those other substances there is no matter of greater temperance or less dross than in these two bodies <note>Gold and silver</note> in which the staining rays <term>radii tingentes: the active powers that allow one substance to color or transform another</term> are present, which you may use for staining. But you will not stain with others, since it was said before that they contain within themselves a foul and combustible sulfur, not of a virtuous nature like that found in these two. For all art is powerless unless it has a pre-existing nature which it may follow. You could, however, purge the imperfect metals with lesser minerals; yet when they were purged, they would not possess a golden or silvery nature within themselves. This is because the golden decoction, or digestion <note>The alchemical process of "ripening" metal through heat</note>, was not in them as it is in these two bodies, nor was their sulfur so mature. Therefore, these immature things must be aided by that which is mature, so that they may be ripened. 

Consequently, they do not stain, but are stained; for the tincture of gold or silver has a proportional nature in them, because they drew their origin from Mercury <note>original: "ex Mercurio"; the philosophical quicksilver believed to be the root of all metals</note> along with them. From these things it is clearly evident that the lesser minerals cannot stain. For if the imperfect metallic bodies—which agree with Gold and Silver on the part of Mercury—cannot stain, nor infuse a golden or silvery nature, how then could those things do it which do not agree in any nature with them? And therefore, one must not stain except with those things in which the power of staining resides. 

Stain, therefore, with Gold and Silver, because gold grants a golden color and nature, and silver a silvery one. For this reason, you should despise all other things, since in them there is no fruit, but only the loss of things, as well as of time and labor.

# THE CORRECTORIUM

### That gold cures infirmities, and about other metallic bodies. Chapter 14.

<note>The "Correctorium" is a title often associated with alchemical treatises intended to "correct" or explain the true nature of chemical transformation.</note>

Since gold holds such a reputation among both common people and the aforementioned philosophers, it is said that while remaining in its primary state, it cures leprosy <note>In medieval texts, "leprosy" often referred to a wide range of chronic skin diseases or even "corruption" within the body or other metals</note> and possesses many other virtues. This is solely due to its complete digestion, because the excellence of the fire acting within it consumes all the evil humors existing in sick bodies, whether they arise from hot or cold causes. 

But Silver cannot do this, because it does not possess such a great superfluity of fire, and it is not so digested and cooked by natural maturity. Nevertheless, notwithstanding this, it possesses a fiery nature within itself secretly and virtually, but not so fully, because as of yet the fire does not overcome the other elemental qualities as it does in gold. And therefore Silver, remaining in its primary state, does not cure leprosy so powerfully, unless it is further digested by art <note>The "art" refers to alchemy or laboratory processing</note> until it attains the highest degrees of Gold and all maturity. 

For this reason, other sick metallic bodies <note>The "sick" or "imperfect" metals like lead, tin, copper, or iron</note> cure infirmities even less, according to how much they differ from these in perfection and maturity. One differs less, another more, and according to this they cure less; this is due to the defect of infected, fetid, and burning sulfur from which they were made in the nature of their coagulation from the beginning. Therefore they do not cure, since the fire within them is so infected with elemental dregs and is burning, with an admixture of other elemental qualities. ### That there are only two particulars which are true in this art, the first of which is in Mercury, Chapter 15.

<note>The "particulars" refer to specific chemical processes or substances that lead to a partial, rather than universal, transformation of metals.</note>

First, I declare universally to all observers into whose hands these present writings may come, that in the entire sequence of this art, there are only two particulars which achieve perfection according to the philosophers and nature. This is despite the fact that deceivers perform infinite sophistries, whitenings, and reddenings <note>original: "dealbationes, & rubificationes," referring to the stages of the alchemical Great Work</note>, by which the faithful are deluded. The first particular, both in the white and in the red, exists in Mercury <term>Mercury: the liquid metal quicksilver, viewed by alchemists as the "mother" of all metals</term>, without the administration of the perfect medicine, although the body with which it is perfected contains within itself its own particular tincture <note>a "tincture" is the color-changing essence of the alchemical stone</note>, if it is moved by art and operation as nature requires. 

The first thing that is perfected in nature particularly from both species is this: since Mercury is the primary matter <term>materia prima: the fundamental substance from which all things are made</term> of all metals, composed of an exceedingly sulfurous white earth and clear water, the whiteness of the earth shines through the clarity of the water, and the color in it becomes the brightest white, as experience teaches. And since this is immature, it is possible for the Sun and Moon <note>original: "Solem & Lunā," the alchemical terms for Gold and Silver</note> to be made from it. Whence the philosopher <note>likely referring to Aristotle or Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: Let it be mixed with other metallic bodies, because they are of its own matter, and they themselves were generated from it; and therefore, through that artifice, one can transmit a digested nature into it,

And thus, by the metals in which it is embraced, it becomes like them without any foreign admixture; for nature simply rejoices in its own nature, and not through any other foreign medium. That is to say: with the Sun <note>original: "sole"; refers to Gold</note> it becomes Gold, with the Moon <note>original: "Luna"; refers to Silver</note> it becomes Silver, with Venus it becomes Copper, and so with the others. This occurs because each one sends its own power into it, and also because it contains within itself its own good, immature sulfur, which is matured through the Art <note>The "Art" refers to alchemy, the process of accelerating natural maturation</note>. For this reason, other metals—coagulated and stained by sulfur in their particular ways—cannot become Gold and Silver on their own. 

The first reason is this: if imperfect metallic bodies were transformed and mixed with Gold and Silver, then their Mercury would still retain that previously held "bad sulfur." Even if they were cleansed, they could not be purified to such an extent that they would be reduced back into Mercury as they were before such superfluity existed; nor could a perfect body be dissolved within them. And since a perfect body cannot be dissolved in it—the natures on both sides being locked away—each would be separated from the other during the examination <note>The "examination" refers to the trial by fire or cupellation to test purity</note>. This is because it would not possess a hidden perfect nature within itself through which their proper solutions could be perfected by means of the Art, so that other perfect bodies might assist with their own nature, which is naturally perfect. 

The second reason: if they were joined to perfect bodies while undissolved, they could not become Gold and Silver. Since their natures are naturally locked by coagulation on both sides, and since there is no medium opening those natures, the power of one cannot be joined to the other in a natural union. Nor can they be sent into one another so that they return into the Mercury from which they both drew their origin. Therefore, through...

# RICHARD THE ENGLISHMAN

As the philosopher says, "and like is made by like." If indeed those bodies which participate in its nature—namely the imperfect metals—cannot perfect it, then much less can those things which are not of its nature, nor participate with it in mineral power, such as you seek in various dungs <note>Alchemists often debated whether organic materials like dung or hair could be used to create the Philosopher's Stone; Richard argues here for a strictly mineral approach.</note>. And therefore, it is specifically possible for silver and gold to be made from it <note>referring to Mercury</note>, and not in other bodies, as you have heard. **Note.** There is a twofold solution <term>solutio: the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid state</term> of bodies into Mercury. Namely, by Mercury into Mercury, and into Mercurial water. The first solution is required for particular works <note>small-scale or specific transmutations</note>. The second for universal works <note>the creation of the "Universal Medicine" or Elixir</note>. The first solution of bodies into Mercury is nothing other than the resolution of the congealed; that is, that which was locked is opened by solution alone, on account of the entry of one nature into another, and this resolution is used in particular works. The second solution is into Mercurial water, and this is for universal works; and this is not achieved by the mere solution of immature sulfur into Mercury, but through the putrefaction <term>putrefactio: a stage of breakdown and decay intended to purify the matter</term> of the body and spirit in heat and moisture. Since the putrefaction of all things bound together by nature is a solution and separation, the parts bound to one another are thus separated, so that each part is set apart from the other. And this is done through the solution of the elements which are connected in the generation of Mercury, namely water and earth. And these same parts, when they have been purged in their nature, are joined together through conversion, and they love each other more after their purification than before. Although this separation cannot occur in bodies except through the spirit. And thus art transcends nature in one way: that artificial things are made suddenly, whereas natural things were previously made only over a long duration.

# THE CORRECTOR

Do not believe that these are the common elements, such as the water of a cloud and similar things; rather, "water" refers to the moist, "earth" to the cold, "air" to the hot, and "fire" to the dry. <note>The author is explaining that alchemy uses the four elements—Earth, Air, Fire, and Water—as philosophical qualities or states of matter rather than literal substances.</note> And thus they exist within the natures of elemental things, since art <note>In this context, "art" refers to the alchemical practice or human skill.</note> can by no means separate the parts so naturally that they are simply transformed back into the elements as they were before, since nature first changed one quality into another. In such a way, art can indeed separate them well, so that the moist is separated from the dry, and the cold from the hot.

But nevertheless, one quality still possesses the nature of another in some part due to their natural mixture; through this, they can be joined together again just as they were divided. For if one quality did not participate in the nature of another—namely, water in the nature of earth through coldness, and air in the nature of water through moisture, and so on for the rest—then it would follow that the natural work would be totally destroyed. The elements would then be "simple" <note>Pure, unmixed states.</note> just as they were before the generation of Mercury. <note>Mercury, or "Quicksilver," was considered by alchemists to be the "mother" or primary seed of all metals.</note>

And art would have destroyed nature, beginning from the "head"—namely, from Gold and Silver—down to the "first," which is Quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note>, and beyond those principles to the simple elements as they were before the generation of Mercury; however, such a remote thing is impossible in the art. And if it were possible, it would then follow that art would compose the elements anew outside of the first matter (namely, the Mercury of metals) and would generate Mercury again just as it had destroyed it, which is impossible to be done artificially. But art does indeed destroy from the head down to the feet—that is, to Mercury—building up from the feet to the head in a more subtle form of natural substance than it was before. In this way, the species of things are divided.

Copper contains within itself a clean Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium mundum"; in alchemy, Mercury represents the metallic principle of fluidity and luster</note> to some extent, except insofar as there is a defect in its sulfur. This is because it possesses a foul and combustible sulfur; in as much as it is combustible, it burns. It possesses a redness not by reason of "digestion" <note>original: "digestionis"; the alchemical process of maturing or perfecting a substance through heat</note> but by reason of its red and impure sulfur. Nevertheless, the Mercury has more substance than the sulfur, and therefore it fails more slowly in the fire than lead or tin. This is because the Mercury resists, except insofar as it suffers violence from the sulfur mixed with it.

And as for the fact that it is burned more quickly by means of lead, this is by reason of the imperfect Mercury of the lead. Because infected Mercury with infected sulfur—such as lead is—seeks something close to its own imperfection. When silver and copper are mixed together, the lead does not find any infected thing in the silver as it does in the copper, where it first finds the burning sulfur to which it more quickly joins itself. 

In a universal mixture, the Mercury of the copper is more greatly infected. Since lead is infected and more "evil" <note>original: "malum"; here meaning base, reactive, or spiritually/physically unrefined</note> in both parts—namely in its Mercury and its sulfur—it adheres more quickly to the evil than to the good. And insofar as a greater evil clings to an evil, it will be to that extent weaker and worse. Therefore, it clings more quickly to copper than to silver, infecting and burning it. Since the natures of copper and silver, as you have heard, are locked <note>original: "serate"; likely meaning fixed or stable</note> on both sides, they cannot come to the aid of the worse part. And thus copper is burned away from silver, as they were joined in a fluctuating manner. Naturally, however, their natures are locked on both sides. And so lead successfully burns the copper away from the silver, which is separated more slowly without lead; for the more it is burned, the more it will be weak and combustible. ### Concerning the universal way, a general discourse. Chapter XVIII.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'D' containing a miniature portrait of a scholar or philosopher holding a book and gesturing towards the text.</image-desc>
Having concluded the prologue of this art and its particular applications <note>The "particulars" refer to limited chemical recipes that only work on specific metals rather than a general transformation</note>, we shall now speak of the universal way, in which art imitates nature. And this is done in a "dewy bath" <note>term: "balneo rorido," a gentle steam bath or water bath used for slow heating</note>, by means of putrefaction <note>The process of breaking down a substance through warmth and moisture to "kill" its old form</note>, so that the bodies may be dissolved by the viscosity of the Mercurial water. Whence Parmenides says: When the permanent water is joined into one with that which was there from the beginning, there follows the division of the elements and their purification. Whence Albertus Magnus says: Four are made from one, and four become one. That is, from the Mercurial water. The third step is the cleansing of the earth, concerning which Morienus the philosopher says: When this water rots with its earth, the entire mastery <note>term: "magisterium," the successful completion of the alchemical process</note> shall be directed by this. The philosopher says: join the dry with the moist; the moist is water, while the dry is earth. Afterward follows the sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it vaporizes, then cooling it back into a solid to purify it</note> of the earth, about which the philosopher Parmenides <note>An ancient Greek philosopher often cited in medieval alchemy as an authority on the nature of being</note> says: Sublimate that which has been whitened with a swift fire, so that the spirit which you find within it may depart, and the earth may remain calcined <note>Reduced to a powder by heat</note>. Regarding this earth, the philosophers Parmenides and Morienus <note>A legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist</note> say: Do not despise the ash which is at the bottom, for it is the crown of your body, and the ash of things that endure. Thus are the four elements prepared, as you have understood above. Do not join them before their purification, since they would separate on account of their uncleanness; as Ascanius says: Spirits are not joined to the body until they have been perfectly stripped of their impurities.

And the white and red ferment <note>The "yeast" or catalyst used to stabilize the alchemical transformation</note> are joined according to whether the elements are white or red. If they are white, then fire is required. If they are red, then the elements are turned red through fire, so that the fire may digest, mature, consolidate, and absorb the filth of the waters during the union. Let it possess the proportional virtues of the four elements: of earth in coldness and dryness, of water in coldness and moisture, of air in moisture and heat, and of fire in heat and dryness. Fire and earth are the extreme elements. Water and air are the middle elements, which you must join through due and true weights, so that they may love one another more than before. First join the earth with the water. Second, join the air with the fire. And in this way, convert the natures, and you will find what you seek. Then the earth is fit for dissolving, the water effective for cleansing, and the oil or air—in which the spirit is carried—is fit for mixing. The fire is for tinting <note>The final stage of coloring the metal, often associated with the production of gold</note>. Thus the body retains the spirit, just as the spirit retains the soul, with the addition of the ferment.

### Admonition: Two types of deceivers to be avoided, and that the art consists in fixed Mercury. §. 11.

But truly, truly, many <term>pseudo-philosophers</term> <note>original: "pseudophilosophi"; false practitioners of alchemy</note> will come after me who will lead workers astray. Among their kind, I find only two types who cover up this science. The first is ignorant of the art and a <term>sophist</term> <note>original: "sophisticus"; here meaning one who uses clever but false arguments or deceptive materials</note>. The second, however, is knowledgeable but an envious philosopher. 

The first composes deceptive books, testifying to his own frauds and sophistries, and he writes the titles of good philosophers at the head of them so that they might seem to contain the good art and the <term>perfect elixir</term> <note>original: "elixir perfectum"; the medicinal or transformative substance sought by alchemists</note>. And so that they may be more believed by men, they carry around powders of stones, white or red, and they handle gold and silver; but those who follow them fail in their operations when they test those writings. 

The second type is entirely envious, and he has composed books about those things which are most remote from the truth, in order to lead men away from the true path as much as he can. He strives to prove his sayings through mere reasons which seem most certain to the foolish. He places the art in herbs, and the fruits of plants, and in many strange and remote vegetables. Or, so that he might seem to leave us the true art, he speaks more philosophically, taking his foundation upon the <term>four elements</term> <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, which are the <term>philosophical matters</term> <note>original: "materiae philosophicae"; the fundamental substances of alchemical theory</note>, and these by many...

Know this, and do not let it be forgotten: wherever you find it, hold it to be the "greater stone," to which nothing else is similar, nor can anything else do what it does. If it is corrected, it corrects; if fixed, it fixes; if liquid, it dissolves; if thick, it coagulates; if dyed, it dyes. For it excels all other bodies in purity. And whoever could endure the labor of the fire could make from it—along with its own congealed sulfur—a most excellent elixir <note>The "elixir" refers to the transformative substance capable of transmuting base metals into gold or silver</note>. And I shall write whatever I have proven, or done, or seen. I hold nothing from the sayings of the philosophers at present, except that they affirm my own words; for I shall speak the truth, and I have been made free from envy <note>In alchemical literature, "envy" refers to the practice of intentionally obscuring secrets to prevent the unworthy from understanding them</note>. Therefore, let him who wishes to understand my words.

# THE ROSE GARDEN

In the first chapter, I shall describe all the operations that emerge from the matter with divine assistance, and so forth. No deceptive <term>sophistry</term><note>In alchemy, "sophistry" refers to fraudulent or superficial methods that mimic gold without true transformation.</note> shall enter this book; I will always set down the rule that leads to perfection. ->Concerning the Calcination of Saturn and Jupiter. Section II.<-

<margin>Saturn and Jupiter</margin> <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for Lead; Jupiter is the name for Tin.</note> Saturn and Jupiter are calcined first with the help of fire and the skill of the craftsman. This is done with a fire that does not exceed their point of <term>fixation</term><note>The state where a substance becomes solid and resistant to fire.</note>, in a strong earthen vessel, stirring with an iron rod until they are reduced to ash. These ashes are then soaked with sharp, cleansing waters. To produce the red color, purified human urine, "blood water," or red vinegar is useful. To produce the white color, white vinegar, common salt water, alum water, and many other bitter substances are useful. After soaking, they are dried by the fire or the Sun until they have reached the state of a white or red lime.

Likewise, they are calcined with the help of salts, and that calcination is good; also through the help of <term>vitriol</term><note>Sulfate minerals, often used for their acidic properties.</note> and other sharp substances. They are also calcined with the aid of sulfur or <term>orpiment</term><note>A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, and that method is better. But they are best calcined with Mercury in this manner: first, they are <term>amalgamated</term><note>Blended into an alloy with mercury.</note>, ground, and washed with sharp liquids until perfectly purified. Then, they should be mixed with sharp salts by grinding, and with alums and other bitter things; then dried and scraped. Finally, the saltiness should be removed by washing. However, let the Mercury be treated with salt before it is dried...

### On the calcination of Venus and Mars. Section III.

Venus <note>Copper</note> and Mars <note>Iron</note> are calcined with the aid of fire. First, in a reverberatory furnace <note>A furnace that reflects heat onto the material</note>, if their filings are placed inside, they are calcined by the reflection of the flame. From Mars is made "Saffron of Iron" <note>original: "crocus ferri"; iron oxide</note>, which is called the cement of iron. From Venus is made simple burnt copper, or *burnt copper* <note>original: "χάλκος κεκαυμένος" (chalkos kekaumenos)</note>. They are also calcined through heating to redness and quenching in sharp liquids until they are totally converted into scales, just as Jupiter and Saturn are calcined by the removal of their dross; then the lime is soaked with sharp and salty substances until it becomes red and clean. The lime of Venus and Mars can also be whitened. They are also calcined with sulfur and orpiment <note>Arsenic trisulfide</note> mixed with plates or with their filings, and even with salts, alums, and other corrosives. The lime is then prepared by washing and drying until it is as desired. They are also calcined very well by heating to redness and quenching in Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>; whatever can be scraped off in each quenching is scraped with a knife, and the work is repeated until it is as desired. It is then prepared by washing and drying with salts and by drawing off the Mercury, and it will become an excellent lime. And know that the lime of a body <note>A metal</note> is not fixed unless it is calcined with fire. I say this because all bodies can be calcined over the vapors of sharp substances, or with sharp substances themselves. But the better calcination of bodies is done with Mercury.

# THE ROSARY

### On the calcination of the Sun and the Moon. §. IIII.
<note>The "Sun" and "Moon" refer to Gold and Silver, the two perfect metals in alchemy.</note>

The Sun and Moon are calcined <note>Calcination: the process of reducing a metal to a fine powder or ash through intense heat.</note> in the same manner as Venus and Mars <note>Copper and Iron</note>, but what is better and most excellent is to do so through amalgamation with Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>, followed by washing and drying, or by the removal of the Mercury through sublimation <note>The process of heating a substance until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note>, just as has been described. However, the spirits <note>Volatile substances like sulfur or arsenic</note> cannot be calcined unless they have first been fixed <note>Fixation: making a volatile substance stable under heat.</note>.

### On the calcination of other things and mixtures. §. V.

Many other things are also calcined in order to extract the tincture <note>The essential color or transformative essence</note> from them, and so that their parts may be refined and cleansed. And know that while any body may be calcined by itself, if certain things are joined and calcined together, a lime <note>The powdered residue left after calcination</note> is produced that is wonderful in its effect. Do not forget this; experiment, and keep that which is best. This suffices regarding these matters.

### On the sublimation of spirits. §. VI.

Both spirits and mineral mediums are sublimated with assistance. Spirits are sublimated either by salts, or by vitriols <note>original: "atramentis" - metallic sulfates used as dyes or reagents</note>, or by alums, or by bodies <note>metals</note>, or by a mixture of these. And note, that sublimation is performed for the sake of the purification and fixation of the tincture. If spirits are sublimated with impure things, they become fouled. If they are sublimated with substances that cling, they remain more fixed with the tincture below, which is what we seek. Whence it is necessary that they be cleansed first by sharp substances <note>Acids or corrosive salts</note> and by washing, or by a single separation of the impure from the pure. Think diligently upon this. For that medium is a secret. Sublimate the cleansed spirits with the pure limes of the bodies until they are fixed, and you will see that I have spoken the truth.

### On the sublimation of imperfect bodies. §. VII.

Bodies are sublimated <note>Sublimation: the process of heating a substance until it turns into vapor, then collecting the purified solid that forms as it cools.</note> with the help of fire, and specifically through the outward pressure of fire. This is done to obtain a material that is cleanly tempered. For that which is excessively volatile, along with any unclean earthiness, is separated through sublimation; what remains is the tempered substance we seek, as I have stated. They are also sublimated with "elevating agents," such as sulfur, orpiment <note>Arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral used as a pigment and in alchemy.</note>, Mercury, and other spirits. I say this regarding non-fixed bodies, such as Jupiter <note>Alchemical symbol for Tin.</note> and Saturn <note>Alchemical symbol for Lead.</note>, which can be sublimated without dross or any other substance, or with any of the aforementioned agents. Venus <note>Alchemical symbol for Copper.</note> and Mars <note>Alchemical symbol for Iron.</note> are also sublimated with the same agents.

### On the sublimation of perfect bodies. §. VIII.

But it must be especially noted that fixed bodies can also be sublimated—namely, the Sun <note>Alchemical symbol for Gold.</note> and the Moon <note>Alchemical symbol for Silver.</note>. The reason for elevating them is so that we may purify them, either with sulfur, orpiment, or quicksilver <note>Mercury.</note>, which causes them to ascend more quickly through repetition, and allows them to be fixed more swiftly. This is an intimate secret, which I tell you for a certainty, and which almost everyone else conceals. I say this: Bodies must become incorporeal <note>original: "incorporea"; meaning to turn a solid into a gas or spirit.</note> in their ascent, and the incorporeal must become corporeal in their descent. The greatest labor of the art is to make a spirit out of a body, and vice versa. But it is true that if the quantity of the volatile exceeds the quantity of the fixed, it will finally return into a spiritual body, either white or red. Truly, I am not envious <note>A common alchemical phrase meaning the author is not "hiding" secrets out of spite, but is being transparent.</note>, for I have stripped the matter bare.

### On Distillation. Section 10.

Many things are distilled to assist in this work. Water is distilled from green or Roman Vitriol <note>Iron sulfate, often used as a starting material for acids</note>, from saltpeter <note>Potassium nitrate</note>, and from feathery alum <note>A fibrous form of aluminum sulfate</note>; this water is of the greatest value for the assistance of this work, for with it all raw and calcined bodies, as well as calcined or fixed spirits, are dissolved in a wonderful and beautiful solution. Many other waters and oils are also distilled from salts, inks, alums, and many other things—mineral, vegetable, and animal—just as is found in the books of the philosophers who treat this art.

### On Solution. Section 11.

All bodies and spirits are dissolved with the aid of the aforementioned corrosive water, or with other corrosive waters which are made in many ways. Because such things are found quite truthfully and openly in many books of the philosophers, we are excused from treating them in this, our *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosarius"; likely referring to the title of the work, "The Rosary of the Philosophers."</note>. But hold this fast, my friend: that the best solution is made in the fire, in the heat of manure <note>A common alchemical method for maintaining a steady, low heat</note>, and with living Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> and the water of life <note>original: "aqua vitae"; likely referring to concentrated alcohol or a potent solvent</note> once it has been washed; though in the beginning, it is called a poison or a mortified thing.

# MINOR WORKS

### On Waxing (Ceration). §. XII.

Calcined bodies <note>Bodies reduced to powder through heat</note> are "waxed" or softened by combining them with dissolved substances. This is done through a process of imbibing and softening. Although there are many ways to soak these bodies, the best method is performed with Mercury—specifically when it is purified "living water" <note>original: "aqua uiua depurata"</note>. The superior softening occurs with "living azoth" <note>A term for the essential transformative agent or universal solvent</note> and "drop of soap" <note>likely a reference to a specific alkaline substance or a stage of surface tension in the liquid</note>. For the "water of the body," once the body has been reduced into Mercury, is called "blood." Furthermore, in whatever way something is softened with oils, it is worth nothing unless the oil has first been fixed and made incombustible. This specific oil is obtained only from fixed metals; know that this is a most excellent secret, and one found to be most precious among the philosophers.

### On Coagulation. §. XIII.

All dissolved things are coagulated <note>thickened or solidified</note> with the help of fire, and this must be done in firmly closed vessels. But keep this secret from me: a thing is perfectly coagulated when it flows <note>melts</note> under suitable heat and withstands the test of the fire. If it does not, repeat the work, and through the iteration of the task, you will arrive at your goal, the Lord permitting.

### On Particulars for the White Work in General. §. XIIII.

Behold, I have described to you all the true and necessary operations in the labor of this art to shorten the work and assist nature generally. Now, to satisfy your needs, I will explain the best specific and particular methods in this chapter. First, therefore, I will discuss how bodies are augmented <note>increased in volume or potency</note>, and afterwards, the shortening of time and labor, and the elixir. And because the true Red <note>The final stage of the Great Work, the Rubedo</note> can in no way be made unless the White <note>The Albedo, or silver stage</note> precedes it, such things are indeed for augmenting the white roses <note>A poetic term for the white tincture or silver-making stage</note>...

### Concerning the particulars for the red in general. §. XVI.

Let us proceed to the augmentation of "red roses" <note>the red or gold stage of the alchemy, known as the Rubedo</note>. The first general rule is this: place the Sun <note>gold</note> into every red work, just as you placed the Moon <note>silver</note> into the unleavened mass <note>original: "azymo," referring to the base metallic starter</note>. But it must be noted that the calxes <note>powders produced by heating a metal in air</note> of certain bodies are turned red by the aid of fire alone, while others are not. Those which are turned red are these: the calx of Mars <note>iron</note>, of Venus <note>copper</note>, and of Saturn <note>lead</note>. However, the calx of the Moon <note>silver</note>, of Jupiter <note>tin</note>, and of fixed Mercury is not turned red by the aid of fire alone in this first chapter. But in our second and final chapter—namely, in the Great Mastery—their calx is turned red at will, and they provide color beyond measure. Behold the treasure of the philosophers!

Nevertheless, in this first chapter, they are turned red with coloring agents, such as sulfur, vitriol <note>original: "atramentum," a term for metallic sulfates</note>, iron-water, and the red philosophical oil extracted from minerals, vegetables, or animals. The method of operating is the same as in the white work of the Moon, but in this work, the Sun <note>gold</note> must be calcined and dissolved. All non-fixed calcined bodies shall also be dissolved. Once they are turned red through that same calcination in corrosive or dissolving waters—I mean the reddest waters—join the waters together and congeal them. Descend them into a red mass, just as you did with the white, and repeat this work fifteen times, as you did with the unleavened mass.

### A Particular [Recipe] for the Red specifically. §. XVII.

Wash filings of Mars <note>original: "limaturam Martis"; iron filings</note> in warm salt water, then in warm fresh water, and finally in vinegar many times—say, twenty times—until it becomes clear and well-cleaned. Place it in a glass or glazed vessel with the best white vinegar for several days, until it becomes very red through this process, which will happen quickly. Then the whole is placed in a glass still <note>original: "distillatorium"</note> and distilled repeatedly until those filings totally disappear. For they will undoubtedly be sublimated with the aforementioned vinegar, and all those filings will pass into a red water. Let this stand in quiet for several days; this water tints prepared and molten Moon <note>original: "Lunam"; referring to Silver</note> wonderfully into a red color. In every repetition of the work, soak the metallic ashes with this water, dry, dissolve, congeal, and refine them until the tincture is sufficient. This water is both mineral and corporeal.

### The composition of strong water, which is the key of the Rosary. §. XIX.

## Section XXI. The Seclusion of the Rosary by the same water.

## SECOND CHAPTER

### That Mercury alone is the cause of perfection. Section 1.

It was stated above that the final intention of this most precious art is to improve imperfect metals and lead them to the highest grade. Their imperfection and corruption proceed from a lack of good and pure **fixed quicksilver** <note>original: "argenti uiui fixi"; quicksilver (mercury) that has been made resistant to heat</note>, as I have said many times, and as all skilled philosophers say. It remains, therefore, that this substance alone is the perfecting agent. Let us choose it, then, and let us perfect it, just as they then did...

For example: Gold <note>original: "Sol" (the Sun), the alchemical symbol for gold</note> is made from pure living Mercury, and it returns again into Quicksilver through ingenuity, and thus it must happen for all bodies.

->A likeness suggesting the universal path. Section III.<-

Do not all things that are born, or plants that have come forth from the earth, always return to the earth? And after these have been in that same earth and have rotted over time, then the whole becomes earth again. But that new earth does not have the same virtue as before. For we see that grain is born from the earth, having a stalk and many seeds; and if the stalks are placed back into the earth by a farmer after they have become manure, we see that the whole of the manure returns to earth through putrefaction <term>putrefaction: the chemical breakdown or "rotting" of a substance, seen by alchemists as a necessary stage for rebirth</term>. But if the reserved seeds are placed again in that same earth of their aforementioned stalks, they are increased much more, as is well known to experienced farmers. Thus, bodies submerged in Mercury return through proper putrefaction into the Quicksilver which they were previously; and afterward, the metallic seeds, cast into that same rotted earth, are multiplied and grow beyond measure.

# THE LESSER WORK

->The method of acting is truly as follows, and is entirely according to nature.<-

Our quicksilver <note>original: "Argentum uiuum"; mercury</note>, congealed or thickened by the power of unleavened <note>original: "azymi"; likely meaning pure or unfermented</note> sulfur or red non-burning sulfur, must first be cleansed of all filth and superfluity that can be removed by ingenuity. That "ingenuity" is sublimation, which is done in this way: Let the stone be placed in an open vessel over a moderate fire, stirring the Mercury itself so that all the superfluous moisture—which is accidental to it and by which the work would be corrupted—may fly away. Do not omit this step. 

Then there will remain (after all the watery and undigested material, which was too volatile, has been set aside by a fire that does not overcome its radical fixation) a substance tempered between the fixed and the non-fixed, suitable for completing this work. 

And let there be a seed or ferment <note>The "ferment" acts like a starter in bread-making, transforming the base metal into the desired substance</note> most purely purged, of which one part is sufficient for twelve parts of the purged stone. Let an ingenious amalgamation of both be made. Then, let the entire amalgam be placed in a very strong glass vessel with a narrow neck, or in an earthen one capable of sustaining the density or compaction of glass (which is better), and let the mouth be firmly sealed. 

Let a large and thick philosophical furnace be built, in the middle of which is placed a very strong, wide, earthen vessel capable of enduring the fire. In that vessel, all the containers holding the matter are to be placed. Then let the furnace be covered, and let it be closed at the top with a thick lid. Let there be three or four holes in its summit for directing the furnace, and let a slow fire be applied persistently. A "slow fire" is defined as one that cannot overcome the fixation of the stone.

# THE ROSARY

And the control of the fire <note>Latin: *ignis regimen*; the precise management of heat is considered the most difficult part of alchemy</note> ought to be such that the lead would remain continually melted within it. And this alone I manifest to you. For by such a control, you shall have complete putrefaction <note>The breakdown of the initial matter into a black, fertile state</note> in one hundred and twenty-four days. Blackness, moreover, is the approved sign of putrefaction. 

Furthermore, through the aforementioned control, you shall have the second sign, which will be a redness lasting for thirty days; indeed, in those days it will be perfectly completed. The third sign, however, is greenness, which will be completed in the heat by the aforementioned control in seventy days. Truly, between the third sign and the fourth, all colors that can be imagined will appear. Then the marriage, the coupling, and the union of the spirit and the soul takes place there; for then they dominate together, whereas previously each was by itself under its own sign. That is to say: in the first sign the body was dominating, in the second sign the spirit, and in the third the soul. 

The time of the union, with the control of the heat slightly increased, will be entirely completed in seventy days, and the fourth sign will arrive, which will be a useful fermentation <note>original: *azymatio*; likely referring to the "leavening" or preparation of the white stone</note>. With the increased control, one hundred and forty days will pass, and the sign of whiteness <note>original: *albedo*; the penultimate stage of the work</note> which we spoke of will be complete. 

If you afterwards continue the control with an increase of heat, you will see between the fourth and fifth signs discolored ashes; let them nevertheless be dear to you, for God will restore liquefaction to them by pouring in His fiery spirit. And you shall see, when God wills it, the fifth sign, decorated with an unspeakably splendid clarity and redness. Fear God, and honor Him with your substance.

# MINOR.

### On the properties of the perfect tincture. §. 5.

Many things indeed have been recounted in this Rosary of mine <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> for the sake of obtaining knowledge of the Work, and to introduce those who are ignorant to the mastery of truth. And because nothing superfluous is placed within it, I do not wish to send it forth diminished. * Look upon the complete red, and the red diminished from its redness, and every redness of the fixed and the non-fixed, of the dead and the living, of minerals, vegetables, and animals; look upon the living that gives life, and the dead that brings death, the white that whitens, and the red that reddens, and that which brings the imperfect to perfection. Moreover, in as much as the whiteness of the perfect [substance] is increased, to that same extent it tints into whiteness, and likewise concerning the red. 

But note, and consider what kind of bodies these are, and what can be applied to them in their liquefaction <note>The process of melting or becoming liquid</note> that might persevere with them and remain through the examination <note>The "test" or "trial" of the fire, usually involving cupellation to check purity</note>; for not every unleavened thing, nor every red thing, tints bodies into the Moon <note>Silver</note> and the Sun <note>Gold</note>. The tincture of the body must be such that it may be mixed with the liquefied body, and enter into that liquefied substance just as the body itself would do with the same. Therefore, the tincture ought to be a corporeal substance, extracted from bodies, or augmented by the benefit of mineral, vegetable, or animal mediums, always within a corporeal thing. 

The truest tincture of whiteness, therefore, is sulfur <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" often refers to the active, combustible principle or the "soul" of a metal</note> from the Moon <note>Silver</note> made most white; and the most perfect tincture of redness is sulfur from the Sun <note>Gold</note> made most red. Therefore, one is just as possible as the other. The prudent and discerning craftsman knows this.

IF by the aid of crude, cold, and moist quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; mercury</note>, and through its benefit, the hot, dry, and clean sulfurousness is extracted—which burns all things because of its scorching power—there remains pure quicksilver, cooked within the bodies and congealed by the force of the sulfur. Thus, by the aid of some quicksilver, the purest sulfur is extracted from the Moon <note>silver</note> or the Sun <note>gold</note>, and there remains an unleavened or red sulfur, which tints blackness and is fixed. One part of this tints two, or three, or four, or six parts into Moon <note>silver</note> with the aid of the first part. Truly, one part of the red tints two, or three, or four, or six parts of the quicksilver cooked in the first chapter—according to the purity of that quicksilver—just as with the white. 

In the second and final chapter, however, one part of the sulfur of the Moon or Sun tints a thousand parts of the body—that is, of the cooked quicksilver. The power of this sulfur is so greatly increased through the industry of the craftsman, with fire or with aid, that after its completion it tints over a thousand, or a thousand thousand and beyond; nevertheless, all things are perfected by fire alone. For every tincture, whether white or red, must receive its color from the fire; otherwise, it is of no value. 

The "aids," however, are such stones with which the purity and fixation of the tincture are increased: namely, eggs, hair, blood, quicksilver, sulfur, orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note>, sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride</note>, vitriol <note>original: "atramentum"; ink or metallic sulfates</note>, alum, saltpeter, borax <note>original: "tinkar"</note>, tutty <note>zinc oxide</note>, marcasite, magnesia, and others. sufficient for completing the work by itself. For there are aids, and as it were helpers, with which, and with whose assistance, the bodies are cleansed and rectified, tinted and completed. They act as co-helpers and mediators for the joining of bodies. Among these, the most precious and best found by us have always been eggs, hair, and the blood of a young male. From these, the four elements are extracted, which, after they have been rectified <note>Rectification refers to the process of purifying a substance through repeated distillation</note>, supply what is lacking in the elixir prepared from metals. Neither the metals by themselves, nor the stones, are brought to perfection. Instead, the elements extracted from these four <note>referring to the organic materials mentioned above</note> are placed in the stone to serve as the oil, or as the tinted soul. The lime <note>term: calx; the powdery residue left after a metal has been "burnt" or calcined</note> of the metallic bodies is prepared to serve as the unleavened or red body. The spirit, whether white or red, is extracted from the bodies, or is fixed and prepared from the spirits themselves. If the stone is washed and cleansed, fixed, tinted, and rectified by these other stones, the work is hastened. Indeed, from the proportioned mixing of the aforementioned prepared substances, a new form results; and thus the elixir is made, insofar as the matter is more digested and tinted than the natural Sun <note>original: "Sol naturalis"; in alchemy, "Sun" almost always refers to gold</note>.

GRACE be to God, the creator of all things, who has guided and sustained us, and taught us, and given us understanding and knowledge. Unless the Lord guarded and guided us, we would be without protection and without a teacher, like those who wander in error; indeed, we would know nothing of this world unless He Himself taught us, He who is the beginning and the knowledge of all things, by His power and goodness over the people. He directs and instructs whom He wills, and by His mercy leads them back to the path of justice. For He sent His messengers into the darkness, and explained the ways, and by His mercy filled those who love Him. Know, brother, that this our <term>mastery</term> <note>Latin: magisterium; refers to the completed alchemical process or the "Great Work"</note> of the secret stone, and this honored office, is the secret of the secrets of God, which He has hidden from His people, nor did He wish to reveal it to any except those who, like faithful sons, have earned it, and who have recognized His goodness and greatness. For whoever seeks the secret of God, it is necessary for him to have this secret of the mastery more than any other.

The philosophers of old have reported these things in their books. And I have spoken of certain matters which they themselves concealed, and which they by no means wished to speak of or record in their writings. I have also explained and set forth certain things which they covered up with their obscure and figurative sayings. I have called this work of mine *The Book of Alchemical Secrets* <note>original: "Secretorum Alchemiae"</note>. In this book, I have named whatever is necessary for the seeker of this science, or mastery <note>term: "magisterium" - the complete process for achieving a specific alchemical transformation</note>, using language suited to his understanding and the senses of the inquirer.

In this book, I have named four masteries that are higher and better than those the wise men of the past achieved. Of these, there are Elixirs—one mineral and another animal—while the remaining two are mineral processes but are not elixirs. One of these is the art of washing, which they call "the bodies" <note>likely referring to the purification of base metals</note>. The other is to make gold from living mercury <note>original: "azot uiuo" - a term for quicksilver or the essential spirit of mercury</note>, the making and generation of which follows the same order of generation found in the mines existing in the heart and bowels of the earth.

The wise men explained these four masteries and arts in their books concerning the composition of this work. However, much was missing from their accounts, and they were unwilling to include the actual operations in their books; or, if a seeker did find them, he could not understand them, finding nothing more difficult than that. Therefore, in this my book, I shall describe the operation itself and its execution.

Whoever reads this book of mine should also read something of geometry and learn its measurements, so that he may correctly construct the design of the furnaces <note>original: "clibanorum"</note>, neither exceeding their proper proportions by increase or decrease. He must also know the quantity of the fires, and their manner or even their degrees...

### Concerning the four masteries of the art, namely: solution, congealing, whitening, and reddening. Chapter 1.

<note>The "mastery" or magisterium refers to the completed alchemical process or the Philosopher's Stone itself.</note>

I begin to describe the greater art, which they call Alchemy, and I shall verify my statement; I will hide nothing, nor will I remain silent here concerning it, except for that which is not fitting to say, nor to be named. <note>Alchemical authors often claimed to reveal all secrets while simultaneously asserting that certain "divine" steps must remain veiled from the unworthy.</note> We say, therefore, that the greater art consists of four masteries, just as the wise men have said: namely, Dissolving, Congealing, Whitening, and Reddening. And these four quantities are participants, of which two are likewise participants with each other, and similarly the other two. And each of these double quantities has another participating quantity, which is the greater participating quantity after these two. And I wish to say, regarding these quantities, the quantity of the natures and the weight of the medicines, which are dissolved and congealed in order, where neither diminution nor addition enters. But both of these, namely solution and congealing, shall be in one operation, and they deserve a single act, and this is before the composition. But after their composition, the work will be different; however, this solution and congealing, which I have named, are the solution of the body <term>corpus: the solid metallic base</term> and the congealing of the spirit <term>spiritus: the volatile substance, often mercury or sulfur</term>, and they are two, yet they have one operation. For the spirit is not congealed except by the dissolving of the body, and likewise, the body is not dissolved except by the congealing of the spirit. And the body and the soul <term>anima: the mediating life force in the chemical wedding</term>, when they are joined...

### On Decoction and its Effect. Chapter 4.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial letter 'E' depicting a scholar or alchemist seated at a desk with a book and instruments.</image-desc>And you should know that the philosophers have named "decoction" <note>original: "decoctionem"; a process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or change its state</note> in their books. And do not transgress what I tell you in this book, and you shall proceed rightly. Afterwards, nature works upon it within man with its own heat, and renders it into flesh and blood. And our operation of the mastery <note>original: "magisterij"; the "Great Work" or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> is like this. Whence our seed, which is regarded by the wise in such a way, has its perfection and its process through fire, which is the cause of life and death; it does not grant life to it except through an intermediary and its spirituality, which are not mixed except with fire. Now I have verified for you the truth, which I have seen and performed myself.

And let him likewise understand the quantities of the fires, and what is beneficial to this matter, and what is harmful to it. It arises from the benefit and the harm of the fire. Whence Plato said in his discourses, in his book: Fire adds benefit or progress to the perfected, and harm or corruption to the corrupted. <note>Plato is frequently cited in medieval alchemy as a philosophical authority, though the specific quote likely stems from the "Turba Philosophorum" rather than his known dialogues.</note> Whence, when its quantity is good and suitable, it will be beneficial; but when it is multiplied in things beyond measure, it will corrupt both—namely, the perfected and the corrupted alike. And those things are the waters made from calxes <term>calx: an oxide or powder produced by roasting a metal or mineral</term> and salts, the preparations of which are found in the books of the wise concerning this mastery. And some of the wise have named them "sea waters," and "milk of birds," and similar things.

# THE EMERALD
## TABLET OF HERMES TRIS-
->megistus <gloss>concerning alchemy <note>original Greek: περὶ χυμείας</note></gloss>. Translator unknown.<-

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'V' depicting a seated figure (possibly Hermes) beneath a large bird (eagle or phoenix), with landscape elements and figures in the background.</image-desc>The words of the Secrets of Hermes, which were written upon the Emerald Tablet, found between his hands in a dark cave in which his buried body was discovered. It is true, without falsehood, certain, and most true. That which is below is like that which is above. And that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of the one thing. And just as all things were from one, by the mediation of the one, so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation. Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon. The wind carried it in its belly. Its nurse is the earth. The father of every <term>perfection <note>original: telesmi; refers to the completed work or "talismanic" power</note></term> of the whole world is here. Its power is complete if it be turned into earth. You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently and with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again it descends to the earth, and receives the power of the higher and lower things. So shall you have the glory of the whole world. Therefore all obscurity shall flee from you. This is the strong fortitude of all fortitude, which will overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing. Thus the world was created. From this shall be wonderful adaptations, the manner of which is this. Therefore I am called Hermes Trismegistus <note>meaning "Thrice-Greatest Hermes"</note>, having the three parts of the philosophy of the whole world. That which I have said concerning the operation of the Sun is completed.

And note: the Philosopher <note>likely referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary author of the Emerald Tablet</note> calls the operation the father of every *telesmi* <note>original: "telesmi"; a Greek-derived term meaning a perfection, secret, or completed treasure</note>, that is, of every secret or every treasure of the whole world—meaning every stone found in this world. It is here. It is as if he says, "Behold, I show it to you." Afterward, the philosopher says: Do you wish for me to teach you when the strength of the stone is perfect and complete? Namely, when it has been turned into its own earth. And therefore he says: **ITS POWER IS ENTIRE,** that is, perfect and complete, **IF IT HAS BEEN TURNED INTO EARTH.** This means if the soul of the stone itself, which was mentioned above (for the soul is called wind and air, in which is the whole life and strength of the stone), has been converted into the earth—namely, the earth of the stone—and is fixed. Thus, the entire substance of the stone becomes one with its nurse, which is the earth, so that the whole stone is turned into a ferment <note>a leavening agent or catalyst</note>. Just as in the making of bread, a little ferment nourishes and leavens a great quantity of dough, and so converts the entire substance of the dough into ferment. In this way, the philosopher intends that our stone be so fermented that it acts as a leaven for the multiplication of the stone.

### On the Purification of the Stone. Chapter VII.

<image-desc>Decorative initial letter 'C' showing a scholar or philosopher seated and gesturing toward the horizon, symbolizing the beginning of the practical work.</image-desc>
Consequently, he sets forth how it ought to be multiplied. But first, he describes the purification of the stone and the separation of its parts, saying: **YOU SHALL SEPARATE THE EARTH FROM THE FIRE, THE SUBTLE FROM THE GROSS, GENTLY WITH GREAT INGENUITY.** Gently—that is, little by little, not through vio-

# COMMENTARY

...but with ingenuity, namely in the philosophical dung <note>original: "fimo philosophico"; a term for the gentle, moist heat used in digestion or fermentation processes</note>.
You shall separate, that is, you shall dissolve. Because dissolution is the separation of parts. The earth from the fire, the subtle from the dense.
That is, the dregs and impurities from the fire, air, and water, and from the entire substance of the stone, so that the stone remains there most pure and without filth.

->That the non-fixed part of the stone must overcome<-
->the fixed part, and elevate it. Chapter VIII.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'E' featuring a floral or foliage pattern within a square frame.</image-desc>And the stone thus prepared is suitable for multiplication. And now he sets forth its multiplication and its easy liquefaction through its power of penetration, as much in hard bodies as in soft, saying: **IT ASCENDS FROM THE EARTH TO THE HEAVEN, AND DESCENDS AGAIN TO THE EARTH.** Here it is greatly to be noted, that although our stone in the first operation is divided into four parts, which are the four elements, nevertheless, as was said above, two of its parts are primary. One which ascends upward, which is called "non-fixed" <note>volatile</note>, and the other which remains below "fixed," which is called earth, or the ferment, which nourishes and leavens the whole stone, as has been said. Truly, of that non-fixed part, it is necessary to have a great quantity and to give it to the stone—which has been made most pure without filth—so many times through the mastery <term>magisterium: the technical process or expert practice of alchemy</term>, until the entire stone is carried upward by the power of the spirit, by sublimating and refining. And this is what the philosopher says: it ascends from the earth to heaven.
