# THE GARDENER

### How the volatile stone must be fixed again. Chapter IX.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'P' containing a seated figure, possibly a philosopher or monarch, framed by foliage.</image-desc> Afterwards, it is necessary for this very stone, having been so exalted <note>raised to a higher spiritual or chemical state</note>, to be waxed <term>incerari: the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</term> with the oil extracted from the stone itself during the first operation, which is called the "water of the stone." It must be roasted by sublimating <note>turning a solid into vapor and back to solid</note> it so many times until, by the power of the fermentation of the earth exalted with it, the entire stone descends once more from heaven to earth, remaining fixed <note>stable and resistant to heat</note> and flowing. And this is what the philosopher <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> says: IT DESCENDS AGAIN TO THE EARTH, AND SO IT RECEIVES THE POWER OF THE SUPERIORS by sublimating, AND OF THE INFERIORS by descending. That is to say, that which is corporeal shall become spiritual by sublimating, and that which is spiritual shall become corporeal by descending.

### Concerning the fruit of the art, and the efficacy of the stone. Chapter X.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial 'S' entwined with ornate floral and leafy vine patterns.</image-desc> THUS YOU SHALL HAVE THE GLORY OF THE WHOLE WORLD; that is, by means of this stone so composed, you shall possess the glory of this world. THEREFORE ALL OBSCURITY SHALL FLEE FROM YOU. That is, all poverty and sickness. For the stone made in this way is the cure for every ailment. THIS IS THE STRONG FORTITUDE OF ALL FORTITUDE. Because there is no comparison of other strengths of this world to the strength of this stone. FOR IT SHALL CONQUER EVERY SUBTLE THING, AND PENETRATE EVERY SOLID THING.

# COMMENTARY

IT PENETRATES. It will conquer, that is, by conquering it will convert the living Mercury <note>original: "Mercurium uiuum"; likely referring to quicksilver or the volatile principle in alchemy</note> by congealing it; for it is subtle, and it shall penetrate other bodies that are hard, solid, and firm.

### That the Mastery imitates the creation of the universe. Chapter XI.

Afterward, the philosopher gives an example concerning the composition of his Stone, saying: SO THE WORLD WAS CREATED. This means: just as the world was created, so also is our Stone made. For in the beginning, the whole world and everything that was in the world was one confused mass, or a confused chaos, as was said above; and afterward, through the craftsmanship of the Supreme Creator, that mass was divided into the four elements, marvelously separated and rectified <note>refined or purified</note>. Because of this separation, diverse things are brought forth. In the same way, diverse things can be made through the adaptation of our work, by the separation of the different elements from different bodies. HENCE WILL BE MARVELOUS ADAPTATIONS. That is, if you separate the elements, there will be marvelous compositions, suited to our work in the composition of our Stone, through the joining together of the rectified elements. OF WHICH—that is, concerning these wonders suited for this purpose—THE METHOD—namely, of operating—IS GIVEN HERE.

->THE GARDENER<-

MEGISTVS. After the philosopher <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> taught the composition of the stone, he here teaches in a hidden manner from what our stone is made. He names himself beforehand so that his disciples, upon arriving at this knowledge, might perpetually remember his name. Then he touches upon that from which it is made, saying: HAVING THREE PARTS OF THE PHILOSOPHY OF THE WHOLE WORLD. Because whatever is in the world, having matter and form, is composed of the four elements. From this, there are infinite parts of the world, all of which the philosopher divides into three principal parts: namely, the Mineral, the Vegetable, and the Animal parts. Concerning these, whether joined together or separately, the philosopher possessed true knowledge in the work of the Sun <note>original: "opere Solis"; referring to the creation of gold or spiritual perfection</note>. And therefore he says, "having three parts of the philosophy of the whole world," which parts are contained within a single stone, namely the Mercury of the Philosophers <note>A metaphorical "First Matter," not common quicksilver</note>.

### *Why the stone is called perfect. Chapter 14.*

And for this reason, this stone is called "perfect," because it possesses within itself the nature of minerals, vegetables, and animals. For the stone is three and one, having four natures—namely the four elements—and three colors: namely black, white, and red. It is also called a grain of wheat, which, unless it dies, remains alone. But if it dies (as was said above) when it is joined in the "conjunction" <note>The chemical or spiritual union of opposites</note>, it brings forth much fruit; namely, when it is com-

# COMMENTARY.

Having completed the operations mentioned above. O dear reader, if you understand the operation of the stone <note>The "Philosopher's Stone," the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life</note>, I have told you the truth; but if you do not understand it, I have told you nothing. WHAT I HAVE SAID CONCERNING THE OPERATION OF THE SUN <note>original: "operatione solis"; in alchemy, the Sun represents Gold</note> IS COMPLETE. That is, what has been said concerning the operation of the stone<gloss>is</gloss> of three colors and four natures existing, as was said, in a single thing—namely, in the philosophical Mercury <note>The "Mercury of the Philosophers" was believed to be the essential "First Matter" of all metals, distinct from common quicksilver</note> alone.

# JOHANNES PETREIUS, PRINTER,
## GIVES GREETINGS TO THE STUDIOUS READER.

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'H' featuring floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

You have before you at present, studious reader, a few small but by no means common works <gloss>concerning</gloss> <term>chrysopoeia</term> <note>original: "χυσοποιϊα"; the art of making gold</note>. If I perceive that these have been pleasing to you, I shall shortly bring to light more and even better works of this kind from among those in my possession. However, since the manuscripts are partly corrupted by age and neglect, and partly distorted by the ignorance of copyists, they cannot be corrected and emended without the comparison of many copies. I ask, therefore, that if anyone possesses any of these works, whether in Latin or in German, they would be willing to generously share them with me. Thus, by comparing many copies, more accurate versions may reach the hands of students. Whoever does this will earn no small favor among the candidates of this art, and shall receive from me several printed copies, along with their own original manuscript unharmed, as a gift. These, moreover, are the works we have in our possession, the best of which we have marked with an asterisk.

* Seven Treatises of Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origins of alchemy and hermetic philosophy.</note>.
* The Dialogue of Mary the Prophetess <note>An early alchemical author, often identified in tradition as Miriam, the sister of Moses.</note>.
* The Assembly of the Philosophers <note>original: "Turba philosophorum"; one of the earliest Latin alchemical texts, presented as a debate between pre-Socratic philosophers.</note>.
* Morienus <note>Refers to Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit said to have taught alchemy to the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>.
* The Book of Distinctions.
* Alphidius. &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; &emsp; Avicenna on Minerals.
  The Light of Lights <note>original: "Lumen luminum".</note>.
